en: 1.1. The section on Brahman:
Brahman is without beginning or end, the essence of speech, the imperishable syllable;
from it proceeds the evolution of the world, as it manifests in the form of objects.
That which is traditionally taught as one alone, by virtue of its reliance on diverse powers, appears as if distinct from those powers, even though it is not separate from them. (1.2)

Depending upon His power of time (*kāla-śakti*), which has superimposed its parts (*adhyāhita-kalā*), there arise the six transformations—birth and the rest—which are the sources of the differentiation of existence. (1.3)
Of that single seed of all, which exists in manifold ways in the form of the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the act of enjoyment. (1.4)
The Veda is the means of attainment and the imitation of that [Brahman]; though it is one, it has been handed down separately by the great seers as if it possessed many paths. 1.5.

The multiplicity of paths for the various divisions, the status of being subordinate members toward a single ritual action, and the fact that words possess their respective capacities—all this is observed within its branches. (1.6)
And the various Smṛtis, which serve both visible and invisible purposes, were formulated by those learned in the Veda based on that very [Veda] through its indicative marks. (1.7)

The various doctrines of those who maintain the doctrine of unity and those who maintain the doctrine of duality have arisen in many ways, based upon its figurative expressions and born of their own conceptual constructions. (1.8)
In that context, purity is said to be truth itself, which is the single-syllable scripture;
it is joined with the form of the *praṇava*, which is not in contradiction with any doctrine. (1.9)
The various branches of knowledge, which serve as the causes for the refinement of wisdom, extend from that Creator as the primary and secondary limbs of the worlds. (1.10)
The wise say that grammar is near to Brahman, the highest of all ascetic practices, and the first limb among the Vedic meters. 1.11.
This is the direct path to that most meritorious light, which is the supreme essence of speech once it has attained its full differentiation of form.
Words alone are the foundation for the reality of the engagement with objects;
the comprehension of the true nature of words does not exist apart from grammar. 1.13.
That gateway to liberation, the remedy for the impurities of speech,
and the purifier of all sciences shines forth as the supreme knowledge.
Just as all classes of objects correspond to their names by being based on the forms of words,
so too in the world this science is the ultimate resort of all sciences.
This is the first station for those ascending the steps of spiritual accomplishment;
this is that straight royal road for those seeking liberation.

Here, one who has transcended all error perceives only the Self as the source of the meters, the Self consisting of meters, and the body composed of meters—[the Self] within the desire [of the meters], by means of the desire [of the meters]. 1.17.
That which is the supreme form of speech, in which all distinctions have subsided—that pure light which unfolds even within this very darkness. (1.18)
Having transcended the perception of forms and activities,
and having passed beyond light and darkness, they worship that which is pure radiance.
In that state, the signs of speech appear like marks for the recollection of syllables, shining forth through a connection preceded by sound, like reflections. (1.20)
In him [are contained] the Atharvans, the Aṅgirases, the Sāmans, and the Ṛg and Yajus;
in whom the high and low syllables abide, each maintaining its distinct position.
That which is one, yet is divided manifoldly through various processes—by resorting to that grammar, the supreme Brahman is attained. (1.22)

In that regard, the great seers—the authors of the sūtras, along with their commentaries (anuttantras), and the commentators (bhāṣyakāras)—have declared that the relationship between words and their meanings is eternal. (1.23)

Those items which are the extracted meanings, those meanings which possess established characteristics, those words which are to be explained grammatically, and those which are the means of communication—[all these are the objects of grammar]. 1.24.

Those relations that exist among grammatically correct and incorrect forms—whether as cause and effect or as suitability—with respect to the linguistic element (*dharma*) and its conditions (*pratyaya*), constitute the constituent parts (*aṅga*). (1.25)
In this treatise, they have been described by means of their characteristics and their own specific terms;
now, only some of them are followed for the sake of memory, in accordance with tradition. (1.26)
Words established by tradition from the learned are correct (*sādhavaḥ*) and are the means for accomplishing Dharma;
however, those that are the opposite, even if there is no difference in their conveying meaning, are incorrect (*asādhavaḥ*). (1.27)
Whether they are eternal or produced, their beginning is not found; and this very state of affairs is called "eternality," just as it is in the case of living beings. (1.28)
No one ought to establish this [linguistic] convention as being purposeless; therefore, the tradition (smṛti) concerning correctness is recorded by the learned. (1.29)
And dharma is not established by reasoning apart from scripture;
even the knowledge of the sages is preceded by scripture. (1.30)
Furthermore, those uninterrupted paths of Dharma which are established, no one subverts them through reasoning, because they are well-known to the world. (1.31)
Since the potencies of entities differ according to the variations of state, place, and time, their establishment through inference is exceedingly difficult. (1.32)
When a substance whose power is already known is related to a particular substance for the sake of this or that causal efficiency, that power is obstructed. (1.33)
Even an object that has been inferred with great effort by skillful inferents may be established in a completely different way by others who are more proficient. (1.34)
The discernment of gems, silver, and so forth, which arises for experts through practice alone and cannot be described to others, is not inferential. (1.35)
Established beyond both direct perception and inference,
the supernatural powers (siddhis) of the ancestors, rākṣasas, and piśācas arise solely from their past actions (karma).
For those whose light has manifested and whose minds are unafflicted, knowledge of the past and future does not differ from perception. (1.37)
Those who perceive with the vision of a seer (ārṣa-cakṣus) entities that transcend the senses and are not accessible to ordinary consciousness—their word is not sublated by inference. (1.38)
How could anyone else turn back one who, like his own property, does not doubt another's knowledge or vision, and who stands firmly on the side of direct perception? (1.39)
Regarding these two categories—"this is merit" and "this is evil"—the utility of the scriptures for human beings is minimal, even down to the outcaste (caṇḍāla). 1.40.
That which exists without interruption, like consciousness itself—by relying on that tradition (āgama), one is not refuted by arguments based on logic (hetuvāda). (1.41)
For one who relies primarily on inference, a downfall is not difficult to encounter, like a blind man running on a rugged path by means of the touch of his hands. 1.42.
Therefore, relying upon the uncreated scripture and the Smṛti together with its foundational basis, the learned compose this Smṛti concerning grammatical correctness. (1.43)
Those who know words recognize two kinds of sounds within the category of "appropriated" sounds (*upādāna-śabda*): one is the cause of words, and the other is employed for the sake of meaning. (1.44)
Undivided, it arises from the divided as the designator of an object; therein the word, whose essence is the form of the object, undergoes a state of fusion. (1.45)
Some who recite the Purāṇas say that there is a distinction between those two;
others declare that the one who is non-different appears as distinct due to a difference in intellect. (1.46)
Just as the fire residing in the fire-drill is the cause of other manifestations of light,
so too the word, when present in the intellect, is the distinct cause of various auditions.
That [word] which was previously reflected upon by the intellect and fixed upon a certain object is then assisted by the sound manifested through the vocal organs. (1.48)
Because sound arises in a sequence, it is neither prior nor posterior; though itself devoid of sequence, it appears as if possessed of differentiation through its sequential form. (1.49)

Just as a reflection, though situated elsewhere, appears to follow the activity of the water due to its influence, so too does that property [of the sphoṭa] appear to follow the activity of the bursting and the sounding. 1.50.
Just as the form of the self and the form of the object of knowledge are perceived in cognition, so too the form of the object and its own form are manifested in the word. (1.51)
The sacrificial rite, which is designated by the word "sacrifice," has entered, as it were, into the state of an egg;
its function, taking the form of action, undergoes a sequential division into parts. (1.52)
Just as a form is fashioned on a canvas as the object of a single cognition, so too is a triad observed in the case of a word with respect to another form. (1.53)
Just as the speaker’s prior cognition operates upon the words themselves, so too does the determination of the perceivers arise with respect to those very same words. (1.54)
People do not perceive those [words] which have fulfilled their purpose by serving another, because they have become subordinate to the meaning in certain denotable objects. (1.55)
Just as light possesses two powers—namely, the state of being perceived and the state of perceiving—so too these two exist separately for all words. (1.56)
An object is not manifested by words that have not themselves entered into the state of being objects;
for those words do not manifest objects by their mere existence if they are not apprehended. (1.57)
Therefore, because its form is not yet known, it is asked, "What does it say?
Just so, the intrinsic nature of the sense organs is not grasped when their object is being manifested. (1.58)
Two properties of the word, grasped as distinct and abstracted [from their substratum], function without contradiction as causes for various operations based on distinction. (1.59)

Just as words such as *vṛddhi* and others, being based on their own forms, enter into a relationship with the named objects (*saṃjñin*) through the words indicated by the [technical] markers *āT*, *aiC*, and so forth. (1.60)
In the same way, this word "fire" is based upon the word "fire";
through the hearing of the word "fire," it enters into a relationship with that which is denoted by the word "fire. (1.61)
Whatever word is uttered is necessarily not itself the possessor of the effect;
its capacity to convey another [meaning] is not obstructed. (1.62)
Because it is dependent upon being uttered, the phoneme (guṇa) is not connected with grammatical operations;
therefore, the connection of operations with its [the phoneme's] objects is postulated. (1.63)
Whatever common property is relied upon between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, in each case another attribute is distinguished within those standards of comparison. (1.64)
When a quality that is the cause of excellence is taught as being independent, its state of excellence is understood precisely through the quality upon which it depends. (1.65)
The word that exists as its denotative form—when that too is uttered, its form is distinguished as something other than that [prior form]. (1.66)
Before it is connected with the bearer of the name (saṃjñin), the name has as its referent only its own form;
thus it serves as the basis for both the genitive and the nominative case endings. (1.67)
Because it must have a purpose, the nominative case is prescribed after a word that is a proper name;
and the distinction expressed by "of this" (asya) arises precisely from that same purpose. (1.68)
However, according to some, the individual instance (*vyakti*) is taught as the "own form" (*svarūpa*) of a name;
the universal (*jāti*), being conjoined [with that instance], undergoes the grammatical operations belonging to the universal. (1.69)

Others, however, maintain that in the sūtra the individual instance (*vyakti*) endowed with a name is intended as the object of apprehension; the individual instance, being made known by the universal (*jāti*), presents itself in the specific rules (*pradeśa*). (1.70)
Regarding whether [the world] is an effect or eternal, some are proponents of unity; regarding whether it is an effect or eternal, others are proponents of plurality. (1.71)
Even when there is a division of words, the oneness of the phonemes does not cease;
and even when sentences are divided, a single word is perceived within them. (1.72)
Apart from phonemes, no other word exists; nor does there exist any sentence whatsoever that is distinct from phonemes and words. (1.73)
Phonemes do not exist within words, nor do parts exist within phonemes; there is no absolute distinction whatsoever between words and sentences. (1.74)
Relying upon divergent perspectives, worldly convention is followed;
therein, what is primary for some is the opposite for others. (1.75)

They declare that for the *sphoṭa*, which is itself devoid of temporal divisions yet conforms to the duration of the sounds (*dhvani*), there is a distinction in its manifestation due to the differences in the limiting conditions of its perception. (1.76)

Because there is a difference in their intrinsic nature among short, long, and protracted [vowels] despite their eternity, the duration of the primordial sound (dhvani) is metaphorically attributed to the word (śabda). (1.77)
The primary sound (prākṛta-dhvani) is held to be the cause for the perception of the word-sound, while the modified sound (vaikṛta-dhvani) serves as the cause for its various modifications. (1.78)
But after the manifestation of the word, the modified sounds (dhvanis) bring about a differentiation of its functions;
however, the essence of the sphoṭa is not divided by them.
The refinement belongs either to the sense organ alone, or to the sound alone, or to both;
these are the three theories held by those who maintain that [the word] is manifested by articulated sounds (dhvani). (1.80)
The refinement of the sense faculty itself is achieved through concentration, medicinal ointments, and so forth;
whereas the refinement of the object is for the sake of perceiving its fragrance. (1.81)
If the eye functions by reaching its object, then a refinement (saṃskāra) of both the object and the sense organ is desired through light; that same sequence applies to sound.
Some maintain that the perception of sound occurs through its non-distinction from the form of the *sphoṭa*;
others postulate that the sound is imperceptible and exists independently. (1.83)
Just as a section of a recitation or a verse reaches mastery through repetition, yet that text is not conceptually determined anew with each repetition; [so it is with the Self]. (1.84)
When a word is manifested by sounds through conditions that are themselves inexpressible yet conducive to apprehension, its true nature is determined. (1.85)
When the intellect has had the seed sown by the preceding sounds and its maturation is completed by means of the final sound, the word is apprehended.
And those words which one considers to exist in the interval between what is non-existent, that is merely the incapacity of the perceiver; it is simply a means of apprehension. (1.87)
The imitation of differentiation is a constant affliction of both cognition and speech;
speech has a form conditioned by sequence, while cognition is dependent upon the object of knowledge. (1.88)
Without an object of knowledge, cognition does not abide in conventional usage;
nor is any meaning expressed by speech that has not attained its sequential order. (1.89)

Just as the apprehension of the first number is the means for understanding other numbers despite their difference, so too is the hearing of another word [the means for understanding the meaning]. (1.90)
The manifestors of individual phonemes, words, and sentences are distinct;
yet, even though they are absolutely different, their powers appear as if intermingled. (1.91)
Just as by means of previous perceptions, even from a distance or in deep darkness, one determines an object in one way after having initially apprehended it otherwise. (1.92)
Likewise, when a sentence is being manifested by the causes of sentence-manifestation, the cognition first proceeds in the form of grasping its constituent parts. (1.93)
Just as there is a fixed sequence of transformation in the case of milk and seeds, so too is the order of cognition necessarily fixed for those who perceive. (1.94)
Even among those very parts of the Lord, there is a differentiation of form in the sound according to its sequence;
or else, since [the sounds] are indivisible, one must employ the conceptualization of a distinction between parts as a means.
The genus (jāti) manifested by numerous individual instances is known as the sphoṭa;
by some, these very instances are conceived as the "sounds" (dhvani). (1.96)
The sound (dhvani), though modified by its causes, serves as the means for the perception of the unchanging word (śabda), just like light. (1.97)
Furthermore, manifestation is not invariably established among impermanent things; nor is the manifestation of eternal universals admitted to depend upon their substrata. (1.98)
A connection with place and other factors is observed even for those possessing bodies;
yet, despite the conceptualization of differences in place, there is no difference between the sound and the word. (1.99)
Just as the fixed capacity between the grasper and the grasped is established, so too is it in the case of the manifested and the manifestor, such as between the *sphoṭa* and the sounds. (1.100)
Furthermore, in the world, there exists for each substance a specific cause that manifests odors and other qualities which are perceived as similar. (1.101)
The object to be illuminated follows the differences among the illuminators; this is evident in the case of reflections in oil, water, and so forth. (1.102)

In objects such as a diamond or the surface of a mirror, which possess contradictory dimensions, there is no possibility for entities that have the same form as mountains and the like to exist. (1.103)
Therefore, in the case of phonemes, sentences, words, and so forth, which exist at non-distinct times,
the time of their manifestation and their own [inherent] time are distinguished by the difference in the *nāda*s.
That which is produced by conjunctions and disjunctions through the organs is the *sphoṭa*; others have declared that the sounds born from speech are the *dhvanis*. (1.105)
Whether the sound is small or great, the duration of the *sphoṭa* does not differ;
however, the subsequent series of sounds consists of an accumulation and diminution [of intensity]. (1.106)
Just as from a distance the mere sound of a lamp's flame is perceived, yet in the case of sounds such as those of a bell and so forth, a distinct difference is clearly observed. (1.107)
Due to the impact of a substance, two accumulated [sounds], though distinct as long and protracted, arise when the vibration has ceased;
these sounds are the differentiators of the *vṛtti*.
Even when the articulatory organ is in unstable motion, other sounds arise from the *sphoṭa* itself, just as flames arise from another flame. (1.109)
Some maintain that air, atoms, and cognition undergo the transformation into sound; for indeed, the diversity of views among various doctrines is unsettled. (1.110)
The air, having acquired its activity through effort that conforms to the speaker's intention, attains the state of sound when struck against the articulatory locations. (1.111)
By the power of its cause, which possesses the nature of an accumulation of momentum, even solid forms are broken apart through their collision. (1.112)
Because they possess all powers, the atoms function through differentiation and conjunction;
they undergo transformation into the forms of shadow, heat, darkness, and sound. (1.113)
When one's own capacity is being manifested, the atoms called "sounds," impelled by effort, accumulate like clouds. (1.114)
Now, this internal knower, abiding within the subtle speech-self, undergoes a transformation into the form of sound for the sake of manifesting its own nature. (1.115)
Having attained the state of mind and reached maturity through its own radiance,
it enters the vital breath (prāṇa) and is then fully manifested.
The wind has become the substratum of the reality of the internal organ;
permeated by its quality, it evolves through fire alone.
Dividing the knots of its own self through various forms of sacred revelation,
the vital breath manifests the phonemes and then dissolves back into those very phonemes.
The self, having empowered the objects through the intellect, joins the mind with the desire to speak;
the mind strikes the fire of the body, which impels the vital air.
That sound which has an unceasing flow is not perceived because of its subtlety; like wind [unperceived] without a fan, it is cognized through its own cause. (1.120)
That power which resides in his vital breath and that which is established in his intellect, as it evolves through its various stations, undergoes differentiation. (1.121)

The power residing in words alone is the foundation of this entire universe; for it is through them as its eyes that this world, which consists of manifestation, expands in the form of differentiation. (1.122)
Since the differentiation of sound and so forth is explained by means of sound itself, therefore all varieties of objects are dependent upon the subtle constituents of sound. (1.123)
Those who know the sacred tradition understand that this is a transformation of sound; from the meters alone does this entire universe first proceed. (1.124)
Having divided himself in many ways, that Prajāpati Chhandasya entered him in many ways indeed, through measures consisting of the Vedic meters.
In those men in whom virtuous speech is firmly established, the form of Prajāpati, which is merit, exists in greater abundance. (1.126)
The great splendor belonging to Prajāpati, as if enclosed within vessels,
returns to its own source upon the dissolution of the body of the wise.
This radiant mandala, the abode of manifold prosperity,
having attained its true state, dissolves into primordial wisdom.
In this world, every course of action depends upon words;
even a child understands it through the impressions deposited in him from previous [lives]. (1.129)
The arrangement of the organs, the upward movement of the breath, and the striking against the points of articulation do not occur without the cultivation of sound. (1.130)
There is no cognition in the world that exists without the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge appears as if permeated by speech. (1.131)

If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness, then manifestation itself would not be manifest, for it is that [nature of speech] which possesses the power of reflective awareness. (1.132)
She is the binder together of all sciences, arts, and crafts;
by her power, every object that has been produced is differentiated. (1.133)
This very consciousness of transmigrating beings exists both externally and internally;
it is pure sentience that has not transcended the subtle elements within all classes of living beings. (1.134)
Speech incites all embodied beings toward purposeful actions;
yet upon its departure, this person is seen unconscious, like a piece of wood or a wall. (1.135)

Through the transformation of the apprehension of distinctions, speech itself—having acquired its formal aspects—is declared in all branches of knowledge to be the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti). 1.136.
Not transcending oneness, yet bound to speech, the various divisions of speech such as "cow" and so forth appear as distinct entities. (1.137)
Those who indeed worship Speech—which has six gates, six foundations, six awakenings, and is sixfold and imperishable—transcend death. 1.138.
Just as the agent proceeds toward an effect through differentiation, so too does that very same [agent] abide as the effect itself through non-differentiation. (1.139)
Having divided himself by himself and created various kinds of entities,
the Lord of All, who consists of all things, proceeds as the enjoyer in a dream.

Just as a word is introduced through its own etymological derivation or through common usage, so too does it attain established conventional meaning; for by that [usage], the object is enjoined. (1.141)

Even when the causal sign (*nimitta*) is absolutely non-existent, the determination of the form of an object is observed through reliance on scripture, as in the case of a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*) and the like. (1.142)
They call the speaker’s own self, which abides within as sound, the Great Bull, with whom union is sought. (1.143)
Therefore, that which is the refinement of sound is the perfection of the Supreme Self; one who knows the reality of its operation partakes of that immortal Brahman. 1.144
Having transcended the function of the vital breath and being established in the reality of speech,
he withdraws himself into the self by means of the yoga of sequential dissolution.
Having applied refinement to speech and having established speech within knowledge,
one should analyze its fetters and, having severed those bonds, render it free from bondage.
Having reached the internal light and severed the grasp of the knots,
one proceeds by cutting through the knots to attain oneness with the causal light.
No one ever accepts a scripture that lacks an author;
therefore, when all other scriptures fail, the Triple Veda alone remains established as the seed.
When debates have ceased and other authors no longer exist,
the world does not transgress the Dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti.
If knowledge were innate, there would be no purpose whatsoever for the scriptures.
If dharma is the cause of knowledge, then the sacred tradition (āmnāya) is its foundation. (1.150)
And logic that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures is the eye for those who lack vision;
for the meaning of a sentence does not rest upon the mere form [of the words] alone. (1.151)

"The intention not to speak despite possessing [knowledge], the subservience to another's purpose, and the inferential manifestation of an object"—this manifold principle is analyzed through reasoning. (1.152)
That power belongs to words alone; reasoning which relies upon human beings is a logic that follows words, and it has no foundation in those things that lack traditional authority (āgama). (1.153)
If even a great circle of jars the color of udumbara fruit,
when drunk, could not lead one to heaven, how could it lead one who has entered upon a sacrifice?

Just as visible forms and other objects are observed to possess specific powers according to their respective capacities, so too are words seen to possess such powers in cases such as the removal of poison. (1.155)
Just as their efficacy is understood in that [worldly] context, so too should it be recognized regarding the Dharma.
Therefore, the virtuous should speak with the virtuous for those who seek prosperity. (1.156)

Everyone understands objects whose fruits are not yet perceived by means of scripture; moreover, it is possible to state anything whatsoever in a scripture, even that which is contrary [to reality]. (1.157)
This tradition of grammar is the basis for the memory of the learned, through which the knowledge of correctness is maintained without interruption. (1.158)
This is the wondrous supreme state of the threefold speech—consisting of Vaikharī, Madhyamā, and Paśyantī—which, despite its divisions into many sacred paths (tīrthas), remains one. 1.159.
Like a cow, the goddess Sarasvatī, possessing a radiant smile, flows forth as a single stream of supreme nectar; she is a cow of speech who manifests in both divine and non-divine forms. 1.160.
Behold the interval between these two subtle, vibrating breaths; within the space between the prāṇa and apāna, one [consciousness] eternally abides as the ground of all.
But another exists without being impelled, functioning even without the vital breath;
from that, the vital breath is born again, nourishing speech.
Sustained by the vital breath (prāṇa), that very speech, which is the basis of all worldly transaction, never speaks at any time unless it has obtained exhalation.
The voiced [articulation] proceeds as having an inherent sound, while the unvoiced proceeds without sound;
and between these two, the soundless indeed prevails over the voiced.

When the wind is released through the various locations [of articulation], speech in its manifest form (*vaikharī*)—which assumes the form of phonemes—is dependent upon the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) for its speakers. (1.165)
The middle speech (madhyamā vāk) proceeds by transcending the activity of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti), following the sequence of forms assumed by the intellect alone. (1.166)
But Paśyantī is undivided, with all sequence withdrawn;
she is the light of her own nature within, the subtle and imperishable speech. (1.167)
Though it is constantly being filled with adventitious impurities, like the final digit of the moon being replenished with nectar, it is never completely overwhelmed.
They call that immortal digit the sixteen-fold Puruṣa, upon seeing whose true nature one's qualification [for worldly existence] ceases. (1.169)
Having attained a form colored by adventitious disturbances,
that *vaikharī* speech is not intermingled with them, just as pure *sattva* is not mixed with the [other] *guṇas*.
That [word] is established as being produced through both the differentiation and non-differentiation [of its parts];
however, those who know the intrinsic nature of things perceive the powers of words [to function] in this way. (1.171)
They say that the sacred revelation (śruti) is beginningless, uninterrupted, and authorless; as for the tradition (smṛti), though it is composed by the learned, it is not interrupted. (1.172)
The manifestation of evolved things occurs without division, as is heard [in scripture] like a dream;
however, having discerned the true nature of existence through its signs, the Smṛti has been prescribed.

The impurities that reside within the objects of body, speech, and mind are purified by the medical sciences and the inner treatises (adhyātmaśāstra) which characterize the methods of healing. (1.174)

That word which, being devoid of correct grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), is intended to be used as "gauh" [with the wrong vowel length], they consider to be an *apabhraṃśa* (corrupt form), even though it conveys a specific meaning. (1.175)
Words such as *aśvagoṇī* and others are correct in different domains;
their correctness is established everywhere according to the difference in the underlying cause (*nimitta*). (1.176)
In the case of the virtuous, these [words] become the causes for the arising of conviction through inference;
as if having attained identity with them, they illuminate the meaning of the word. (1.177)
The learned do not follow them, just as they do not follow synonyms;
since they are [treated] by the Smṛti scripture in that manner, they are therefore not directly expressive.
Just as a child learning to speak utters indistinct sounds such as "ambvaṃbu," those who know the truth reach certainty regarding the clear expression through that indistinctness. (1.179)
Thus, when a correct word ought to be employed, if an incorrect form (apabhraṃśa) is used instead, some meaning is expressed by it only through the mediation of that correct word. (1.180)
Through a traditional succession, corrupted forms have attained common usage among speakers who lack proficiency; consequently, for them, the correct form is no longer expressive.
This divine speech has been thrown into confusion by incompetent speakers; however, regarding this doctrine, those who perceive only the impermanent experience a perversion of intellect.
Because there is no interruption between the two, when another word is employed with the intention of expressing something else, that other word is not the designator of the original object. (1.183)
Thus ends the Brahmakāṇḍa in the Vākyapadīya composed by Bhartṛhari.
2. The Section on Sentences:
It is declared that [the sentence] is a collection of words, a genus residing in a collection, a single partless word, or a sequence synthesized by the intellect. (2.1)

Regarding what constitutes a sentence, the views of those who perceive the principles of logic are diverse in many ways: some hold that every word is independent, while others maintain that every word is dependent [on others]. (2.2)

That which is formulated as a technical rule (paribhāṣā) in the treatise for the purpose of establishing the conditions for elision (nighāta) and so forth, does not apply to everything that possesses the same formal characteristic, because it consists of parts that require mutual expectancy. (2.3)

A sentence is said to be that which has parts requiring mutual expectancy, consists of words that do not require further external words, has the action as its primary element, possesses subordinate qualifiers, and expresses a single unified meaning. (2.4)
And that which is a vocative word is a qualifier of the action; thus, in the case of "vrajāni devadatta" (O Devadatta, let me go), there is a *nighāta* (elision of accent) when that is so. (2.5)

Just as even a single word ending in the suffix *ktvā* can be a qualifier for a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), so too, they say that a word ending in a verbal suffix can be a qualifier for another word ending in a verbal suffix in that context. (2.6)
Just as a single light that illuminates all objects is differentiated according to the diversity of what is seen, so too is the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence [differentiated]. (2.7)
Just as a single variegated form is designated by means of distinctions such as blue and so forth, which possess different characteristics, [so too is the one mind designated]. (2.8)
In the same way, the designation of a single sentence that is entirely free from expectancy is followed by other words that possess expectancy. (2.9)
Just as in a word the base, the suffix, and so forth are analyzed, so too is the extraction of words from a sentence possible. (2.10)
The state of having a form similar to other phonemes is observed within the constituent parts of phonemes; and the constituent parts of words stand as if they were similar to other words. (2.11)
The bull, water, and barley-gruel are associated with useless parts;
however, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is the basis for linguistic usage.
There is no division in sound; how then could there be one in the object? It is the ignorant person who, through divisions, perceives a difference in the grammatical derivation. (2.13)
Just as there is no meaning for the word "brāhmaṇa" in the expression "brāhmaṇa-kambala," so too would [proper names] such as Devadatta be devoid of meaning within a sentence. (2.14)
The general meaning, having disappeared, does not persist in the particular;
how can there be the abandonment of what has been grasped? Once it has ceased, where could it abide? (2.15)
If the meaning of a sentence were not denoted by words, then the meaning of individual words would likewise be so;
and this being the case, the connection between a word and its meaning would be lost. (2.16)
Certain particularizing words, which resemble general terms, are manifested to the cognizers through their connection with other words. (2.17)
For them, however, the entire meaning of the sentence is completed with each individual division;
the accomplishment of the meaning, characterized by both the manifest word and its subtle nuances, occurs within the cognizers. (2.18)

That manifest, sequential sound which one recites in a whisper is *vyakta*; but that which is without sequence (*akrama*) is that in which the intellect abides as if having expanded [into a single unity]. (2.19)
Just as a difference in action is not perceived even when there is a specific upward motion, so too is the genus manifested through repeated actions such as whirling and the like. (2.20)
In this way, the Vedic revelation, though possessing similar phonemes, words, and sentences, appears as if identical in form despite the absolute difference of its underlying reality. (2.21)
And in the case of eternal things, how could there be "prior" or "subsequent" in the ultimate sense?
Rather, it is the power of that very same single entity which causes it to appear in such a way. (2.22)

Just as the cognitions "long" and "short" appear at different times despite there being no difference in the object itself apart from the distinction of time, so too is the nature of the phonemes short and long. (2.23)
Time, being eternal, cannot admit of differentiation here by means of mere sequences;
for in the absence of distinct moments (*mātrā*), what kind of sequence could there be? (2.24)
The single intellect that arises from those two is devoid of parts;
for, by its own power, it appears as if divided, reflecting upon [its objects] in succession.
Because of the persistence of sequential enumeration, the etymological definition of that seed which has been deposited within her as being either a plurality or a unity does not hold. (2.26)
But at the time of meditative cultivation, this sequence is non-sequential in its efficacy, by which an object whose distinctions have been eliminated is perceived as possessing distinctions. (2.27)
If those very same phonemes that exist in a sentence were also present in the word,
then within the phonemes there would have to be a division of phonemic parts, just as there is a division of atoms.
Due to the lack of contact between the parts, there would be neither phoneme nor word;
since they are inexpressible, what else could be expressed? (2.29)
But others say that the reality of sound is a single entity manifested through its parts; they likewise maintain the unity of that sound within a sentence. (2.30)
In this way, their internal meaning is revealed by means of those parts;
word and meaning are two inseparable manifestations of this very self. (2.31)

The relationship between the illuminator and the illuminated, as well as the nature of cause and effect, always belongs to that essence of sound (śabdatattva), which is internal and consists of pure consciousness alone. (2.32)

The existence and non-existence of that very [cognition] are established as its capacities, appearing in a sequence despite being non-sequential, serving as the basis for conventional discourse. (2.33)

If the existence of word-meanings is postulated on the grounds that they serve as the means of valid cognition (saṃpratyaya-pramāṇa), then by discarding them when the word-meanings are already established, the consequence follows that [the sentence] would be purposeless. (2.34)
The meaning of "king" is understood through the word *rājan* in its distinct form; however, in a compound (*vṛtti*), another word resembling a verb is employed. (2.35)
Just as when the word "aśvakarṇa" is uttered, a certain specific object is understood even without [the presence of] a horse, so too is the cognition [of the universal] in all [individuals]. (2.36)

In certain cases, when a similarity is postulated due to the transition to another meaning within sentences, the status of being a conventional term (rūḍhiśabda) is understood only from the treatise itself. (2.37)
Even those things that are to be abandoned are taught as means;
moreover, there is no fixed restriction regarding these means. (2.38)
A certain person somehow arrives at an understanding of the meaning; for the distinctions based on sentences may be either combined or separated. (2.39)
When the connection "this is that" is undertaken by the intellect, then even a single phoneme may, in some cases, convey the meaning of the sentence. (2.40)
Whatever meaning is expressed by a word alone, they say that [the word], when situated in a sentence, is the denoter of that much meaning. (2.41)
When a relationship exists, that further excellence which arises is called the meaning of the sentence itself, which rests upon many words. (2.42)
Although it resides in many words, it is completed with each individual division;
like a genus, it is also conceived by others as residing in a collection, just like number. (2.43)

Others, however, understand *sāmānya* (the universal) to be that which conforms to all particularities (*bheda*); through its association with other entities, it assumes the form of those particulars. (2.44)
The relation, by establishing itself in a particular [object], restricts that instability of the [cognition] which arises from its desire for further distinctions. (2.45)
The relationship, being inferable from its effect, possesses no form; therefore, they declare it to be absolutely non-existent in nature. (2.46)
The goal is necessarily accomplished by the means, and the action has a necessary means;
that necessity is manifested through their mere proximity. (2.47)
In that context, a noun functions with expectancy as a subordinate element (guṇabhāva),
while the verbal form requires the causal factors (nimitta) as the primary object to be accomplished (sādhyatva).
The specific qualities that reside within objects are indeed eternal; they are apprehended sequentially, and the sentence is not the expressive agent [of those qualities]. (2.49)
And since there is no other expressive word apart from the mere sequence of sounds, and sequence is a property of time, therefore no sentence exists [as a single entity]. (2.50)
And those possible distinctions among word-meanings that remain unmanifested [in isolation] are revealed when they are brought together; however, this process does not apply to phonemes.
The designation "word" and the designation "sentence" apply merely to the sequential arrangement of phonemes and words; phonetic nature (*śabdatva*) is not admitted for those two. (2.52)
However, although the nature of being a word (śabdatva) is the same [in each phoneme], comprehension is observed to arise from the word (pada);
this [comprehension] does not exist for each individual phoneme. Therefore, the wise know that the meaning belongs to the word. (2.53)
Just as phonemes, though possessing parts, are meaningful when combined even without any denotable object, so too is a sentence held to be [meaningful] in this same way. (2.54)

They say that words, though individually devoid of meaning because they are mere phonemes, become meaningful through their referents when uttered in sequence; thus, the meaning of a sentence is said to have a distinct characteristic. (2.55)
Whether one postulates the eternity of wholes or of universals, they declare that the non-deviant capacity of a single sentence to convey a single meaning is established. (2.56)

Those who advocate for the sentence (vākya) maintain that differences are imagined based on a prior non-difference; however, those who focus on the word (pada) consider non-differences to be preceded by difference. (2.57)
The original form of words is described according to the different types of grammatical operation (*vṛtti*);
the *saṃhitā* is the source of words, or rather, the *saṃhitā* rests upon the words. (2.58)

And if the traditional recitation of words (*padāmnāya*) were something distinct from the *saṃhitā* that demonstrates it, then how could the word-form be established there as permanent, given that it is observed through grammatical rules? (2.59)
Just as the cognition of a word-meaning is not perceived with respect to each individual phoneme, so too the determination of the sentence-meaning is not perceived within the words themselves. (2.60)
Just as the meaning of a sentence resides in the words that function together, so too does the meaning of a word reside in the phonemes that function together. (2.61)
Just as a subtle object of perception, when mixed with another, is perceived together with it, so too a phoneme, when connected with another phoneme, is expressive [of meaning]. (2.62)
Just as a certain meaning is determined from the utterance of a word, so too that meaning is perceived from the proximity of the phonemes. (2.63)

If, by virtue of that which has already been obtained, a subsequent scriptural statement is for the purpose of restriction, and thereby the general rule is set aside by an absolute particularity, [then that is the case]. (2.64)
From the injunction "one should sacrifice," the material is obtained through implication;
it would be set aside by the explicit mention of *vrīhi* rice, and thus there would be no substitute. (2.65)

Therefore, the word "rice" (vrīhi) should establish the specific property of being rice; since it is not contradictory, it does not sublate the general property of being a substance (dravyatva), as its purpose is merely to specify that particular instance. (2.66)
And when that coexisting substantiality has been excluded by him, because particularities are impossible there, no others are observed. (2.67)
Nor are all particularities indicated by the word for action as if they possessed a universal; for a word does not denote every existing particularity. (2.68)

Just as existing qualities such as whiteness and the like are not intended to be expressed there [in the definition], so too are the distinctions that coexist with substantiality not intended to be expressed. (2.69)
Let there be no substitute for a rite that is obligatory, nor for one undertaken for a specific desire; thus, its omission is logically justified. (2.70)
If it is argued that the sentence-meaning is conceived as a specific action itself, then in the absence of the substance, its substitute would be a different action altogether. (2.71)
And when a word whose meaning is already known has its referent established, why is there an inquiry as to "what is this" regarding an unfamiliar term such as *pika*? (2.72)

And that which is obtained through the force of the context and is supplied for the sake of completing the sense of the individual word—this direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), by virtue of being thus supplied, sublates both indicative power (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*). (2.73)

But that which, such as "white" and so forth, is not [directly] obtained yet is understood through proximity—that is brought about by effort within the sentence and is distinct from the property of direct audition (*śruti*). (2.74)

If it is maintained that a sentence is indeed non-different only when its meaning is non-different, then all of that, being established by direct audition (śruti), will not contradict direct audition itself. (2.75)

Furthermore, regarding that collection of sentences which exists for the sake of establishing a single meaning and whose constituent parts are mutually expectant, even the meaning of the sentence does not exist [as a distinct entity]. (2.76)
This is an incidental matter; this is obtained through the *tantra* [method]; this [is obtained] through two types of repetition; here, there are both sublation and combination. (2.77)
In this matter, modification (ūha) is logical; its connection is not to be sublated.
This is an extension (atideśa) of the general rule; here, the specific detail is what is extended.
In this context, "desire" (arthitva) means "capacity"; the meaning here does not differ [from that].
This person has obtained the entitlement through the scripture; his exclusion applies to other ritual actions. (2.79)
"This sequence is obtained through direct Vedic statement (śruti), while this other is from the order of pronunciation;
therefore, this sequence is stronger here, yet it is not intended [to apply] in this case. (2.80)

This [word] is connected with the secondary members (*parāṅga*) and is not the motivator (*aprayojaka*) of the primary members (*aṅga*); this [other word] is their motivator, and here this [latter] is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) with it. (2.81)
"This is the primary [element], this is the subsidiary; this is the sequence of application: this assists it directly, while this distinguishes it indirectly. (2.82)
In this case, there is a distinction between the capacity and the operation; however, it is the result that differs here.
This difference in cognition arises from the relationship; the distinction therein is not intended to be expressed.
"This is a non-presuppositional negation (prasajyapratiṣedha), while this here is an exclusionary negation (paryudāsa);
this is secondary (gauṇa), this is primary (mukhya); this is pervasive (vyāpin), and this is heavy (guru) or light (laghu). (2.84)
Through differentiation, its relationship as part and whole is conceptualized in many ways; this is restricted to that, and here its fitness arises. (2.85)
From the indicative mark (liṅga) observed in other sentences, its distinction [from them] is inferred; this word-meaning is then analyzed by being abstracted from words. (2.86)
Thus, those properties within sentences which are based upon the meanings of words would all fail to be established if the word were non-expressive. (2.87)

Even though the meaning of a sentence is indivisible, when it is extracted through a distinction of powers by means of the division into other sentences, what has been stated is not contradicted. (2.88)
Just as there is a conceptual differentiation of a single fragrance in flowers and other things, so too is a difference in meaning expressed within a sentence. (2.89)
Just as in the case of the gavaya and the man-lion (narasiṃha), one perceives a portion of another genus as being similar, even in the absence of a single [unified] cognition. (2.90)
But when a fool perceives a portion that is unestablished, unseen, and not observed, he assumes a lack of consciousness regarding that very extent, and thus concludes it to be so everywhere. (2.91)

Likewise, through the application of words such as "pika" (cuckoo) in a sentence that is entirely distinct [from its referent], one considers there to be a cognition of a non-existent object that is merely similar [to it]. (2.92)
Similarity is perceived in one part and difference in another part, by a partless consciousness directed toward a partless luminosity. (2.93)

In the very same way, similarity is determined in one part and difference in another part, even in the case of sentences whose properties are entirely distinct, despite the absence of any shared parts. (2.94)
If words were destroyed [at the moment of utterance], how could there be the conceptualization of a limit? And if the word has not grasped its limit, how can its meaning be distinguished? (2.95)
Just as the form of colors appears [as one] in a mixture, so too that form, though established elsewhere in sound, is held to be another form through its application across various forms. (2.96)
In that non-difference, the conjunction of differences occurs;
therefore, a form is distinguished as being non-different from another form. (2.97)
In the treatise, the identity of the means of cognition with the object cognized is sometimes relied upon;
at other times, a distinction between the act of grasping and the object to be grasped is maintained. (2.98)
By relying on non-difference through the sound *ū*, [the rule] is conceived according to the respective order;
however, in the case of the inclusion of *lṛ* and *luṭ*, difference is conceived along with the two things to be grasped. (2.99)
The form *yasya* here denotes the designata (*saṃjñin*) of the suffix *aṇ*; for it is not possible for there to be a grasping [of a term] by means of what is merely being implied. (2.100)
The syllable *ū* is thus both non-different and based on different constituent parts;
its perception as distinct is like the "external form" (*pararūpa*) of two [sounds]. (2.101)

Furthermore, by rejecting the expansion of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the *pluta* vowel as well as the combination (*samāhāra*) of vowels, he has resorted to an absolute distinction among words. (2.102)

Just as there is a difference in form among words such as *ardharca* and others according to their sequence, so too, within the framework of a single word, there is a different perception for those [phonemes] that are distinct according to the system. (2.103)
In the context of the *saṃhitā*, phonemes do not change their essential nature;
rather, it is as if they become different words by assuming different capacities. (2.104)

The perception of objects as distinct from one another through the modification of the senses and so forth occurs in the case of audible things [the Vedas] only through the abandonment of the notion of a self; that is the sequential process. (2.105)
Due to the difference in the act of denotation, even though the words themselves remain unchanged, that very same single form appears as if it were absolutely distinct. (2.106)
The *sāman* is either the *ṛc* itself or merely the melody; it is not a separate substance.
However, due to the differences in melody, those very same *ṛcs* are perceived as modified. (2.107)

In the compendium of the Vedas, it is stated in the treatise that when words which have been split apart by means of a grammatical operation and subsequently remain as a single residue are uttered together again, they possess correctness (*sādhutva*). (2.108)

Having adopted a single grammatical rule (śruti) even for those [phonemes] that possess different forms, their simultaneous utterance (tantra) must be performed; otherwise, they would not be correct. (2.109)
And when sentences of identical form are pronounced by means of *tantra* (abbreviation) without being explicitly taught by the grammatical treatise, a single correct form is obtained. (2.110)
Just as a single [mantra] assumes multiple forms through the adoption of different tubes and so forth, in the same way, many [mantras] may possess a single form by virtue of the tantra. (2.111)
Just as there is the occurrence of sentences consisting of distinct words, so too, even in the absence of other separate sentences, these [words] would possess individual meanings. (2.112)
If the meaning of a word were the denotable object and the purpose were the meaning of a sentence, then for such a [view], no connection between sentences would be possible. (2.113)
In that case, it is the verbal roots alone that require one another; however, the relationship [between them] is understood as being connected to those verbal roots. (2.114)
In the conceptualization of the distinct meanings of words, there is either repetition or restatement;
for while the meaning is complete in each individual word, it functions [as a whole] when the words occur together. (2.115)
Regarding the meaning of a sentence as free from conceptual construction, various conceptualizations based on mental cultivation arise;
in this context, the debates of former masters are held in many ways. (2.116)
Others maintain that every word is a cause of intuition through repeated practice, as is observed in the communication of meaning to children and animals. (2.117)
And some maintain that this convention (*samaya*) is a practice (*abhyāsa*) without prior source (*anāgama*), which demonstrates: "This effect follows immediately after this [cause]. (2.118)

"There is an object for all words"—this is the definition of that which is to be communicated; they say it is the same as in the case of *apūrva*, deities, and heaven, even in the case of words such as "cow" and the like. (2.119)
However, that apprehension of form which arises from the practice of observing [the object] during application is not the object of the word, for it depends upon a different effort. (2.120)
Some distinctions are manifested by words that denote them; it is held that certain word-meanings arise as concomitants [of those primary meanings]. (2.121)

When a word conveys a universal (jāti), the individual (vyakti) is necessarily associated with it; however, the word denoting the universal does not rely upon the specific distinctions residing in that individual. (2.122)

A word does not convey the specific forms of jars and other such things, because it is applied to the mere entity; therefore, the cognition of those [forms] is necessarily dependent on something else. (2.123)
An action prompted by a word is not observed to occur without its application; therefore, it is understood that the meaning of a word is the application which follows as a consequence. (2.124)
However, others maintain that those applications which are fixed and that means which is fixed are what are denoted by words. (2.125)

Some maintain that the meaning of a word is either a collection (*samudāya*)—whether it be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) or a mere aggregate (*samuccaya*)—or else it is a relation (*saṃsarga*) that is unreal. (2.126)

Either that which is real, though possessing unreal adjuncts, becomes the basis for words; or else, the word itself, having attained the state of conceptual identification (*abhijalpa*), becomes the denotable object. (2.127)
When the form of a word is unified with its object through the connection "this is that," they call that word *abhijalpa*. (2.128)
Since these two are not of a separate nature, their conventional usage is non-deviant;
in some cases, a particular form alone remains predominant. (2.129)
In common worldly usage, a word functions having attained the status of an object;
however, in the scientific treatise (śāstra), it possesses both forms, distinguished according to the speaker's intention. (2.130)
Whether due to incapacity or omnipotence, the fixed conceptualization of action and so forth regarding a single object is constructed solely by means of words. (2.131)
Alternatively, that object which is the domain of the intellect and is based upon an external thing, being known as "the external thing," is understood to be the meaning of the word. (2.132)
These [objects] appear as possessing forms, being cognizable, and serving as the basis for manifestation and memory; pure consciousness, however, is otherwise than this. (2.133)

Just as the sense organ, when it comes into contact [with its object], manifests a variety [of perceptions], in the very same way, the comprehension of an object from a word occurs in manifold ways. (2.134)
Furthermore, when speakers proceed in different ways toward various listeners, the meaning of a word is differentiated according to the conformity with each individual's own cognition. (2.135)
Even regarding this visible object, individual perceptions differ;
and even a single person perceives it differently again after the lapse of time. (2.136)
And even for a single word, its meaning is conceptualized in many ways by one person or by many, through various unstable causes. (2.137)
Therefore, for those who have not perceived reality, their vision or even their speech is always faulty, full of deception, and perpetually unstable. (2.138)
And as for that vision of the sages which is established in some degree of reality, there is no worldly transaction by means of it, nor is it dependent upon words. (2.139)
The sky appears as if it were a surface, and a firefly like a flame;
yet there is no surface in the sky, nor is there fire in the firefly. (2.140)

Therefore, even when perceiving an object through direct perception, the wise person should examine it through reasoning; one should not posit the existence of a perceived object merely on the authority of that perception. (2.141)
Just as worldly people provide designations for things whose true nature is inexpressible during conventional discourse, the wise person should not conceptually construct such designations. (2.142)
When the meanings of words are apprehended as distinct, there arises another intuition (pratibhā) which they call the "sentence-meaning" (vākyārtha), brought about by the word-meanings. (2.143)
How could this [nature], which is "this very thing," not be inexpressible to others?
Established as an internal occurrence, it cannot be defined even by its own creator. (2.144)
Not being critically examined, it brings about, as it were, a close contact with objects;
having assumed, as it were, a universal form, it exists as the objective domain. (2.145)

No one can overstep that [Vedic injunction] which produces [knowledge] through direct verbal expression or by following from the mental impression (*bhāvanā*), regarding the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*). (2.146)
The entire world follows that [convention] as a valid authority; even the undertakings of animals proceed by its power. (2.147)

Just as the powers of intoxication and so forth are seen to arise without effort from the ripening of specific substances, so too are the flashes of intuition (*pratibhā*) of those who possess them. (2.148)
Who transforms the vocal function of the male cuckoo in spring?
And how are living beings instructed in the construction of nests and the like? (2.149)
In activities such as aversion to food, attachment to pleasure, and swimming—well-established through their species and lineage—who is the instigator for beasts and birds? (2.150)
This [certainty] arises from scripture alone when it is accompanied by meditative cultivation;
however, scripture is distinguished [as more authoritative] by its proximity or remoteness [from the object]. (2.151)

They know intuition (*pratibhā*) to be of six kinds: that which is produced by nature, by practice, by yoga, and by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), as well as that which is distinguished and that which is assisted. (2.152)
Just as the word "cow" is employed when an object is characterized by substances possessing conjunction, yet that word does not reveal those specific qualities themselves. (2.153)
Even though a word functions with respect to cows and other such things that are conjoined with shapes, colors, and parts, it does not admit those [as its actual objects]. (2.154)
A word is applied to an object distinguished by its configuration, color, and constituent parts; its application to any individual part of that object is not observed. (2.155)
For anyone in the world, it is difficult to perceive all the constituent parts [of an object];
however, when certain parts are perceived, the whole object is inferred. (2.156)
Likewise, the determination of the qualities of jasmine, blue lotuses, and so forth—which coexist with their fragrance and are seen to be eternally connected to it—is observed. (2.157)
Independent of number, measure, and configuration, the word for water and other such things functions as a denoter both in a single drop and in a collection. (2.158)

That which is established in oil and the like, which are delimited by their constituent factors (saṃskāra) and so forth, speaks of a single part as the reality itself, while [the object] exists in its constituent parts (avayava). (2.159)
When a designation is employed because it is connected with a specific object, its employment ceases once that object has disappeared. (2.160)
However, when a word is employed having internalized those properties that are possible [to be expressed], it does not necessarily require the actual presence of those [properties]. (2.161)
Just as the word "cow" is seen to apply even when there is deviation regarding such things as hairy hooves, it does not function in the absence of the universal (jāti). (2.162)
Therefore, when there is a comprehension of a possible object from a word, that [object] is understood as being connected with the meaning of the non-perception of its absence. (2.163)
The case endings for duality and so forth may either be expressive of number or they may be the denoters of a referent that possesses number. (2.164)

Alternatively, some say that words such as "cow" and the like denote certain objects—endowed with numerical distinctions—even without the explicit mention of a number, by means of a distinction in their own essential form. (2.165)

Those words whose relationship [to their meanings] is eternal, whose capacities are known through differentiation, and whose meanings are distinguished by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)—[their meaning is thus determined]. (2.166)
As long as it is possible to conceive of those two [the base and the suffix] through an inseparable connection, a restriction applies there;
however, such a restriction does not exist in the case of suffixes such as *nuṭ* and *śa*.
The status of being a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇatva) is postulated for a name only when its application is possible;
for the powers of words are relative and restricted to specific relations. (2.168)
The connection of the meanings "well," "soup," and "sacrificial post" is observed [in the respective words];
therefore, it is understood that the composite whole itself denotes a different meaning. (2.169)
Explanations differ regarding the etymological derivations of words;
when many meanings are possible, some specific cause [for the usage] is accepted. (2.170)
Vairava, Vasiṣṭha, Giriśa, as well as Ekāgārika and others,
have been designated by some in various ways through a confusion of causes and limits.
Just as the description of a path by means of trees, anthills, and mountains is not contradictory, even when [the path] is accompanied by distinct things such as cows and the like. (2.172)
Furthermore, those who perceive differences in states provide alternative designations for things such as the *kiṃśuka* tree, based on the determination of its various parts. (2.173)
By some, various etymologies for the word *gauḥ* have been demonstrated here: from the roots *gṛ* (to swallow), *garj* (to roar), *gam* (to go), *gav* (to seek), or *gad* (to speak). (2.174)
The word "cow" (go) applies to cows either by virtue of its own form as "gauḥ," or it is derived [from a root]; or rather, some maintain that everything is both ways. (2.175)
And in the treatise, a general instruction is adopted for the sake of brevity;
the specific details of another [category] serve as the indicators, just like those of a different genus. (2.176)
And that which occurs in a different sense is known as a different root; it does not, despite having an identical form, become attached to another conventional meaning. (2.177)
The two roots *iji* and *jī* have been designated by some as distinct for different specific meanings; indeed, the methods of exposition are diverse. (2.178)
And thus one should treat Bālavāyā and the others like Jitvarī;
when both difference and non-difference are accepted, there is no contradiction whatsoever. (2.179)

In the grammatical treatise, the separate conceptualization of roots and prefixes is for the purpose of establishing the rules for *aṭ* and so forth; however, in reality, it is the root alone that possesses such [power]. (2.180)
For it is traditionally taught that this rule applies to the root *saṃgrāmayati* when preceded by a prefix;
such specific actions are undertaken within a composite whole. (2.181)
In this way, the internal relationship between the verbal root and the prefix is maintained;
it is precisely such an action that enters into connection with the factors of accomplishment (sādhana). (2.182)
When the means of accomplishment are ready for application, the object to be accomplished is distinguished;
moreover, prior to the connection with the means, the action itself does not yet arise. (2.183)

Just as the status of being a verbal root and the state of being an object are established through the application of a future accomplishment of the root's meaning, so too should other cases be understood. (2.184)
Just as lac-dye and other substances, through their connection at the time of the seed, assist the fruits by means of the transformation of color and so forth. (2.185)
Due to the connection with a verbal root, as well as with prefixes and suffixes, a distinction that was internalized becomes manifest at the time of word-formation. (2.186)
In some cases, distinctions that are possible but not indicated by the roots alone are revealed through their connection with prefixes such as *pra*, *ni*, *ā*, and so forth. (2.187)

That [prefix] is either the designator of specific qualities because they are possible, or it is an illuminator; or else, it is employed as an auxiliary to the verbal root for the purpose of imparting its power. (2.188)

And since movement and so forth are not perceived by means of standing and the other [actions] taken alone, the property of that [movement], such as "setting out" (prādi), is said to be established there through two kinds of inference. (2.189)

When there is no application [of a suffix], and when *adhi* and *pari* denote another action up to what is observed, the verbal root (*dhātu*) together with those two prefixes is devoid of meaning. (2.190)

In the same way, certain suffixes added for their own sake (svārthika), when occurring within a compound and joined with a meaningless element, merely restate the meaning of the base (prakṛti). (2.191)
Some particles are indicators when they are conceived as having distinct meanings, while others, like grammatical augments (*āgama*), accomplish the meaning only when combined. (2.192)
Whether placed above or before, their function as indicators does not differ, even when they are employed in various ways with different meanings. (2.193)

Particles such as *ca* and so forth are not employed in isolation when they possess the status of a word (*pada*); likewise, even though a suffix is expressive, it is not employed in isolation. (2.194)

But when there is a collective expression [of the action], no distinction [between the agent and the action] exists; furthermore, that which has not yet become a substance (asattvabhūta) is expressed by verbal suffixes (tiṅpada). (2.195)
Even when there is a collective expression, words that denote specific meanings are connected with qualifiers; however, particles such as *ca* and so forth are dependent on others. (2.196)
In some cases, having produced a certain relation, an action ceases; in other cases, when an action-word is heard, a relation is born. (2.197)

In that regard, the sixth case-ending is prescribed at the beginning of each [rule] for the purpose of excluding compound formation; however, it is cited as an illustration with respect to the *kāraka* for the sake of showing its application. (2.198)
And that relationship which has arisen when the verbal action has ceased is regulated in various instances by means of a *karmapravacanīya*. (2.199)
That which implies a verbal action is joined with case endings of the kārakas; for example, as in "likhau," where there is the absence of a prefix (anupasarga).

The non-employment of the root *sthā* is also observed, as in the expression *apratyajayan*; furthermore, the root *su* is employed even when used alone in the sense of "facing toward," as in *abhīti*. (2.201)

The status of being a *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed when there is a connection with an action, for the purpose of precluding [the application of rules such as] the substitution of *ṣa* and so forth, in the case of words like *svati* which possess different grammatical properties. (2.202)

When the connection between cause and effect has been delimited by the particle *anu*, the third case ending characterized as a cause (*hetu*) is superseded by the [use of the] ablative (*ārambhāt*). (2.203)
This [particle] does not indicate an action, nor does it express a relation; it neither implies a verbal root denoting action, but rather distinguishes between relations. (2.204)
A collection of meaningless [phonemes] may be meaningful, and likewise, it may be meaningless;
among phonemes, a word is endowed with meaning, but the constituent parts within a word are not. (2.205)
Furthermore, the combination of words endowed with meanings is divided again through the comprehension of a different meaning and through the dissolution of their connection. (2.206)
Some maintain that the meaningful and the meaningless do not attain a relationship when distinct; others, however, hold that they do attain it, citing examples such as a hut and so forth. (2.207)

From meaningful [words], a composite (saṃghāta) arises with a distinct meaning; however, some maintain that it does not arise in the case of compounds, secondary suffixes (*svārthika*), and the like. (2.208)

For some things, whose powers are already known when they exist as separate entities, [their causal capacity] is determined through positive and negative concomitance; others have their capacities merely imagined [through such concomitance]. (2.209)
The meaningfulness of phonemes is indeed demonstrated by the meaning of the treatise itself;
for pure [phonemes] such as *āt* and so forth possess no worldly meaning. (2.210)
The meaning of primary derivatives (kṛt) and secondary derivatives (taddhita), as well as that of isolated [stems], is non-worldly (alaukika);
likewise, the meaning of a word ending in such a suffix does not exist prior to the addition of an inflectional ending (vibhakti). (2.211)
That meaning which is perceived as more clearly manifest at the end of suffixes is of such a nature that it is relied upon because of the context concerning meaningfulness. (2.212)
If there is no distinct entity whatsoever apart from the phonemes in words and sentences, then the phoneme must be the signifier through its power by means of mutual dependence. (2.213)
If a collection [of phonemes] that denotes [an object] were deficient by even a single phoneme, it would not be a different word; therefore, it is understood as being non-deficient. (2.214)
Establishing a memory of the object through that expressive word as the cause, he brings the object—though mediated by the word—as if it were directly present. (2.215)

Just as there is no meaning expressed by the individual words in compounds such as *gaura-khara* and the like, even though a cognition [of the parts] occurs, nothing at all is understood regarding the composite whole. (2.216)

When the essence of an object is perceived as if endowed with the meanings of its constituent word-meanings, the perception of those word-meanings therein is likewise ineffective [in producing that perception]. (2.217)
And when the whole and its parts have different meanings within their respective functions, difference and relation—two contradictory properties—are simultaneously entailed. (2.218)
And who would postulate things such as fire and so forth merely for the sake of a logical proof?
Furthermore, how could there be a meaning in a *bahuvrīhi* compound if its constituent word were not employed [independently]? (2.219)
Nor is there any determination of an object through parts such as "prajña" (wisdom) or "saṃjñā" (perception);
therefore, only the aggregate itself is the basis for the specific object. (2.220)
The word *gargāḥ* is a single term that functions in the sense of many individuals; likewise, a collective compound (*dvandva*) is a group that denotes many things. (2.221)

Just as in the case of *ekaśeṣa*, the action of eating and so forth resides in each [individual], so too the action is distributed individually within the meaning expressed by a *dvandva* compound. (2.222)
And that dependence upon the word *tat* [as a correlative] for the referent of a copulative compound (*dvandva*)—that too is the nature of a pronoun when the object has a distinct form. (2.223)
Just as the act of cutting occurs sequentially in the parts when a khadira tree is being felled, so too is the perception of sequence observed in the constituent parts of a compound object. (2.224)

Just as those who have departed from a portion of the Saṅgha are considered to follow the Saṅgha, so too do they consider specific ritual acts [to apply]; this is the sequence regarding a member of a dual compound. (2.225)
While explaining the function [of words] for the unwise by means of sentences, he has demonstrated in his commentary that primacy belongs to the distinction between word-meanings. (2.226)

Because the referent is non-different, the predominance [of the negative particle] in a *nañ*-compound is described in various ways in the Bhāṣya; however, the faults pertain only to the process of grammatical derivation. (2.227)

And for one who, in the alternative view that [words] abandon their own meaning (*jahatsvārtha*), desires the abandonment of all meanings, the abandonment of the entire referent of a *bahuvrīhi* compound is thereby demonstrated. (2.228)

In some instances in the treatise, the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is expressed by the suffix (pratyaya), and when the base has ceased [to function], the meaning of the suffix is expressed by verbal roots (dhātu). (2.229)

The single meaning that two distinct suffixes express is expressed by the verbal root alone in some cases; for instance, one says "pacanti" (they cook), while in other cases it is expressed by the root even without those two. (2.230)

Furthermore, those meanings of the suffixes which are established as the basis for the traditional grammatical explanations (anvākhyāna-smṛti) have been cited in another tradition as the meanings of the base (prakṛtyartha). (2.231)
It is stated thus in the treatise that [the soul] causes vomiting because of its well-known nature;
for they consider the systematic presentation of the meaning of the treatise to be for the sake of conventional usage. (2.232)

In the treatises, it is ignorance alone that is described through various systematic elaborations; however, true knowledge, being free from traditional dogma and conceptual construction, manifests by itself. (2.233)

Just as a fruit that is unattached to its causes and devoid of any defining characteristics cannot be described, so too knowledge—though it appears through the means of the scriptures—is itself inexpressible. (2.234)
For speech strives to convey a meaning according to habit; and false habituation, established as if it were innate, is beginningless. (2.235)
The unwise person imagines the atom to have parts, and likewise imagines the composite whole to be joined with further parts. (2.236)
Because of the perception of jars and other such objects, the world is determined to be limited; and because of the production of entities, the eternal Brahman must possess a beginning. (2.237)
The skillful means of those in training are for the sake of instructing the ignorant;
by standing upon the path of the unreal, one then strives for the real. (2.238)
Having first grasped the word, one understands the meaning in one way;
yet, subsequently, within the sentence, one understands that very same meaning in another way. (2.239)
Even many objects that have been accepted, when their negation is made at the end, they are thereby excluded; therefore, one should not rely upon them in that context. (2.240)
And the statement "there is no tree" has the characteristic of a qualified absence; neither in the object nor in the cognition does a connection with the exclusion [of the tree] persist. (2.241)
