And if, in the case of the cognition of cessation, it is determined that "it exists," how could that established cognition—which is not denotable by words—be averted? (2.242)

Now, if that cognition which has arisen is rendered false by the negative particle (*nañ*), then how can there be an apprehension of non-existence when the operation of the negative particle is of this [denying] nature? (2.243)
And if it were to function without a substratum, the negative particle would have to function prior [to its relation with the noun];
or else, that very [noun] must be its substratum, and the scriptural mention [of the noun] would serve for the purpose of restriction (niyama). (2.244)

Or, it may be for the purpose of indicating a restriction, or it may be a restatement (anuvāda); in that case, only a certain word would possess meaning, while the remaining words would be meaningless. (2.245)

Furthermore, when a contradictory connection has been established by means of the example and other factors, one understands the meaning of the sentence differently once the sentence is completed. (2.246)
In sentences where praise or blame predominates, the meaning is not such as it is imagined to be through the separate division of the words. (2.247)
Now, the meaning that remains uncombined resides within the individual words;
this is the means for the comprehension of a single sentential meaning. (2.248)
That which was previously unconnected with words and is gradually accumulated, the wise know to be more distinguished because it is like a string of pearls that has been cut and re-knotted. (2.249)
Other investigators say that a single word has multiple meanings; its capacity to signify all those objects is differentiated according to the distinction of the causes [of usage]. (2.250)
Having transcended simultaneity, it settles upon succession, either through the context of the meaning or through connection with another word. (2.251)
Just as a physical body possessing a dewlap and other such features is denoted by the word "cow," so too that very same word "cow" is established even for a Vāhīka. (2.252)
However, because that very word possesses all powers and has multiple properties, its status as primary or secondary arises from the difference in conventional usage. (2.253)
A single mantra exists with distinct powers for the individual self, the deity, and the ritual action; it remains established for all purposes without confusion. (2.254)
Some maintain that the association with "cowness" (gotva) is attributed to the Vāhīka due to a specific cause;
however, it is merely the object that is mistaken, while the word remains established in its own primary meaning. (2.255)
In the same way, the intrinsic form of words is attached to all objects; while the mere object may be inverted, the audition remains fixed upon the intrinsic form. (2.256)

Those who perceive the path of differentiation declare that there is identity between the secondary and primary words because they possess the same form, even though there is absolute difference between them. (2.257)
And in this way, when there is a repetition, it is attached after each *sāmidhenī* verse;
and the mantras acquire distinctness through their application, just like the *ūha* modification. (2.258)

Those very other traditional recensions (āmnāya) are indeed studied; however, there is only a certain portion [of them] that is purposeless, or rather, it is understood that the remainder is something else entirely. (2.259)

The nature of the word is one thing, while the meaning is described differently by others in their recitations; there is absolute difference between all [words], yet those things related to them appear as if they were identical to them. (2.260)

One *sāvitrī* is employed for ritual acts involving formative forces (*saṃskāra*), another is applied in the continuous recitation of prayers; yet she is recognized as being truly one and the same. (2.261)

For one who maintains that words function toward the nature of their referents by virtue of their own form, the sentence as a whole functions toward the sentence-meaning independently of anything else. (2.262)
For those who perceive that a single word has multiple meanings, the distinction between the primary and secondary senses is established based on whether [a meaning] is proven or not proven. (2.263)
Others know that word which, depending on the context of the meaning, or joined with other words, conveys a meaning as being figurative (gauṇa). (2.264)

When a word is uttered in its pure form, that meaning which is understood as its well-known [primary] sense should be known as the primary one; it is based solely on the [phonetic] form itself. (2.265)
But that which is employed as if with effort through the application of another, they consider that to be unestablished, being intent upon a figurative meaning. (2.266)
Even when one is engaged in a primary sense, that which another relies upon as its object is considered the primary cause (nimitta) therein, while the former is regarded as secondary (gauṇa). (2.267)

When two words with contrary meanings, such as "formerly" (*purā*) and "now" (*arāt*), occur in a context where their referents are distinct, their specific restriction is determined by the requirements of the sense and the context. (2.268)
When the meanings of individual words are conceptually extracted from the meaning of the sentence, with which single [word-meaning] could a connection with another word be possible? (2.269)

Furthermore, when a single word is observed somewhere to have the function of expressing an action (*astikriyā*), they say that it is indeed a complete sentence; it is not to be construed with anything else. (2.270)

And when, in response to the question "What is this?", it is said "It is a cow" or "It is a horse," the very act of questioning—the process of perception and so forth—is what has been set in motion therein. (2.271)

Neither the excess nor the deficiency of properties is what determines [the status of a definition]; for some consider even an excess to be [acceptable] due to common usage, while in other cases they regard a deficiency as such. (2.272)
Others understand that word denoting a genus to be figurative when it is employed even in the absence of the genus itself, on account of a property resembling something related to it. (2.273)

Where, due to some semblance of similarity, people perceive as if there were another meaning for an object when there is none, that [usage] regarding cows and the like is called figurative (gauṇa) in certain cases. (2.274)
Just as ploughs, swords, pestles, and so forth, being endowed with specific forms and capacities, are understood to be restricted as the means for accomplishing particular tasks. (2.275)
Nor do their capacities fail to function in other actions; rather, their subservience to that specific purpose is understood with certainty from their very form alone. (2.276)
In the same way, a word that is established through its production by means of form and power, having a fixed denotation, is employed elsewhere by virtue of its [latent] power. (2.277)
Where its capacity is determined by the mere hearing [of the word], that is considered the primary meaning; whereas that which is established through effort is considered secondary. (2.278)

O Venerable One, when the suffix *cvi* is used in the sense of "becoming" (*svārthāt arthāntare sthitau*), the state of that [new] thing is seen there as primary, even though it was previously [not so]. (2.279)
Primordial nature (prakṛti) attains both greatness and the state of purity;
yet, when considered in its differentiated aspects, it is the establisher of secondary status (gauṇatva). (2.280)

Words such as *agni* (fire) and *soma*, which denote their own essential forms (*svarūpa*) as their referents, are employed in connection with the bearers of those names (*saṃjñin*); because [the primary sense] is not established [there], they are used figuratively (*gauṇatā*). (2.281)
But as for the fire that belongs to Agnidatta, there the word [for fire] assumes a secondary (gauṇa) status because it functions with the meaning of "given" (datta) as its subordinate sense. (2.282)
When the process of deriving word-forms has commenced based on a distinction of causes, the presence and absence of the augment *suṭ* are established in the case of *hariścandra* and others. (2.283)

When a word that has already undergone grammatical refinement with respect to its root and so forth is joined with another [word], the internal refinement does not cease even when there is an external referent. (2.284)
Even when an object is determined to be utterly contrary [to its actual nature], the word is used in its primary sense there according to the conventional understanding. (2.285)
Although the determination of the true nature of an object depends upon cognition, not every cognition arises with respect to that object as if it were already well-established. (2.286)
The perception [of water] in a body of water is equal to the perception of a mirage and the like;
however, because of the difference in touch and other qualities, a mirage is not water. (2.287)
Because the specific effects of the rope and the snake are well known, their distinction is determined even though the perception of them is identical. (2.288)
And whatever is seen that has as its cause the reversal of a well-known object—the distinction that is perceived from that [reversal] is declared to be unreal. (2.289)
And just as the depressions and elevations depicted in a painting, along with mountains and other such forms, do not perform functions such as obstruction, so it is in that case. (2.290)

Just as the continuous succession of touches by the hand [is felt] in the case of a wheel, it is not so in the case of a fire-brand circle (*alātacakra*), for that is touched only intermittently. (2.291)
Just as in cities there are no obstructions to touch due to ramparts and walls, so it is not the case even in gandharva-cities. (2.292)

To whatever extent the primary purpose is accomplished by means of actual deer, cattle, and so forth, that same purpose does not exist in clay-made representations; therefore, the suffix *kan* applies to them. (2.293)
A vast region is covered by well-known mountains and the like, yet a reflection is seen as residing within a small portion of space. (2.294)

And just as poison and the like are primary causes for death and so forth, they do not accomplish their own respective effects in dreams and such states; it is the same for the object [in cognition]. (2.295)
Whatever is perceived differently due to variations in place, time, and the sense faculties, that is determined in accordance with the common consensus of the world. (2.296)
The linguistic usage of words, which are based on worldly convention, does not exist by means of either that knowledge born of sensory impairment or that knowledge which is supramundane. (2.297)
Just as a lamp, when employed for a certain purpose among objects such as a jar, produces illumination for other things as well due to their proximity. (2.298)

In the same way, when a word is employed with respect to objects that are associated [with others], it causes those other things to be understood as well, distinct from the primary motivator [of the usage]. (2.299)
Just as the friction-sticks, prepared for the purpose of obtaining fire, produce smoke—which is not the intended result—by means of that same single instrument; (2.300)
Likewise, even when a word is intended to convey a specific meaning, it reveals an unintended meaning as well due to its proximity [to other words]. (2.301)
Just as an object that is utterly intermingled cannot be abandoned, so too a word that is related [to its meaning] cannot be separated. (2.302)
Even when objects are present and even when they are being manifested, it is understood that the object is the motivator of the word, despite there being no difference in its form. (2.303)
In some cases, the status of being secondary or primary among meanings is not intended to be expressed;
in other cases, even their mere presence is not a cause for comprehension. (2.304)
And that which is not directly expressed by the word is understood in some instances;
in certain cases, the primary meaning itself becomes the indicator (lakṣaṇa) of another. (2.305)

Whatever has been stated as an illustration of the meaning of a secondary derivative (taddhita) regarding the relationship between the subordinate and the primary, in that case a reversal is observed. (2.306)
In the case of an explanatory statement (*nirdeśa*), the proximity of gender and number is not a cause [for determining the meaning];
for instance, in the case of "half-a-short vowel" (*ardha-hrasva*) and so forth, a measure (*pramāṇa*) is understood even though it has not been explicitly mentioned. (2.307)

And that which is observed as half of a short [vowel] is designated in exactly the same way even in the absence of that [short vowel], because it serves as the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of the short vowel. (2.308)
Its distinction may be by means of length and protraction, or by its measure;
or it may serve as a definition of the genus, in every way like the *saptaparṇa* tree. (2.309)
"When it is time [to act], one should say, 'The sun should be seen; let it be gone to'; 'Let the time be known'—this is stated as the means [for determining] time. (2.310)
In the phrase "he pierces without a bow," a specific instance is demonstrated;
it serves as a basis for the general capacity, being whatever [agent] conveys that meaning. (2.311)
Even a child, when instructed, "Let the ghee be protected from crows," does not protect it from dogs and such, since the statement is intent upon [excluding] those who would cause harm. (2.312)
Even though it is not explicitly mentioned by its own form, the wiping of the place after washing the bowls is understood as being a constituent part of the act of eating. (2.313)
The meanings of words are distinguished through context, the surrounding topic, the purpose, propriety, place, and time; they are not determined by the mere form of the word alone. (2.314)
Association, dissociation, co-occurrence, opposition, purpose, context, indicative mark, and the proximity of another word [are the factors that determine meaning]. (2.315)
Capability, propriety, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth, are the causes for the recollection of specific meanings when the meaning of a word is otherwise undetermined. (2.316)

Even on the view that [words] are distinct, words—which possess different meanings due to their similarity—reach a restricted manifestation among cognizers by means of context and other factors. (2.317)
Those words which resemble nouns and verbs and are based on other grammatical operations—the meaning of the sentence in their case is not understood from their form alone. (2.318)

A skillful practitioner understands that the conceptualization of praise and blame intended for the purpose of encouraging engagement or discouraging withdrawal does not correspond to reality. (2.319)
Whatever action being enjoined has a visible or invisible purpose, that praise is offered for it; such praise serves as an incentive specifically for the agent of that action. (2.320)
Just as a child is deterred by the mention of a tiger and the like, even though it is unreal, so too is a certain transgression described [as a deterrent]. (2.321)
Even after making preparations, no wise person would engage in an action that is prohibited by the scripture and results in such a transgression. (2.322)
Even after providing protection against snakes through mantras, medicinal herbs, and other means perfected by the Siddhas, one must not act otherwise; one must not cause [the victim] to die. (2.323)
In some instances, the true nature of reality is explained for the sake of praise or censure; even there, engagement and withdrawal are taught. (2.324)

The form (rūpa) of all word-meanings (padārtha) is that which is bound to the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha); however, those sentence-meanings which are dependent [upon others] are equivalent to word-meanings themselves. (2.325)

They consider even that to be a sentence which consists of a single word whose action is already accomplished, because we observe the occurrence of duality at the beginning of a sentence even without an explicit verbal root. (2.326)
Where a specific means (sādhana) is understood from a verb (ākhyāta-śabda), that too is called a single sentence whose meaning is complete. (2.327)
Cognition mediated by words, which relies on words not explicitly uttered, is said to be the cause for the comprehension of that object; it is called inference. (2.328)
Others, however, maintain that this very meaning belongs to the word itself, established independently of its connection with other words. (2.329)
When a particular meaning is understood upon the utterance of a word, they say that very thing is its meaning; there is no other definition of meaning. (2.330)

In the same way that the action of the substituends is understood when words meaning "action" are present as upapadas, so too in a compound with *nir* and other prefixes, the sense of "gone beyond" and so forth is perceived. (2.331)
These are indeed other words, like synonyms used in common parlance; however, their specific meaning is restricted by the context and the purpose. (2.332)
However, those means of awakening which are directed toward this or that particular person are not necessarily connected with the object to be known through the words themselves. (2.333)
Even when there is no actual understanding, or when there is a false presentation, those various words remain established with their respective meanings eternally connected. (2.334)

In this scriptural passage concerning the ritual action, "the door according to the context," whether one should "fasten" or "give" is understood through the means [of the specific situation]. (2.335)
In that regard, a word whose function is to establish [a property] and which is based on a substance does not denote the primary object that is to be proven. (2.336)
Having manifested its own object alone, this [cognition] ceases while still dependent [on that object];
however, its related object brings about its presence. (2.337)
Since the quality of being for the sake of another is not distinct [in this case], there is no proximity of word to word from the word itself;
nor is there proximity of word to meaning from the meaning, nor proximity of meaning to word from the word. (2.338)
If both the action and the substance were to attain primacy simultaneously, then the word expressing the action would be cast aside, as if its form had vanished. (2.339)
However, the verbal nature of this [word] is described as being identical in form to the noun;
its usage is distinguished through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). (2.340)
Nor does the capacity to signify cease even when there is doubt regarding the form; for it is understood through contextual implication, as in the case of the expression "half of an animal. (2.341)
If every locus of a sentient being is pure when bound by conceptualization, and its meaning is not distinct [from that purity] even when differentiated within the context of association. (2.342)
"Verbs have action as their primary meaning, while nouns have substance as their primary meaning; these four classes of words—this [entire system] is contradicted. (2.343)
Having observed that sentences possess eternity in the intellect and worldly connection with meaning, Audumbarāyaṇa asserts that there is no fourfold nature [of the Veda]. (2.344)

And linguistic usage, which possesses pervasion and is indeed concise, based upon words, is conceived through differentiation alone for the sake of practical function in both the world and the treatises. (2.345)
In the world, established conventions do not arise from the mere connection of meanings for those who understand;
therefore, nothing other than the sentence exists that is non-worldly (alaukika). (2.346)
And those [meanings] indicated by signs and sentences heard elsewhere are understood as being their own meanings alone; they remain unperceived because there is no difference in their form. (2.347)
That which was relinquished in the statement of general exclusion, appearing as if wordless though it possesses words, is heard in the subverting statements and is understood elsewhere. (2.348)
Among the Brahmins, the Vedic tradition has proceeded from Māṭhara regarding curd; because of his connection with buttermilk, Māṭhara explains the true meaning there. (2.349)

Even when there is a connection with multiple verbs, some maintain that a sentence—though appearing as if it were divided in form—is intended to be a single unit according to both the general rule and its exceptions. (2.350)
In that case, restriction and prohibition are supplementary to a positive injunction;
when a deletion (*luk*) is prescribed in the second [alternative], they know the non-deletion (*aluk*) to be its supplement. (2.351)

Since they are independent of one another regarding their own cessation and are primary in themselves, how could there be a single unified statement among them, given that they do not assist one another? (2.352)

Because of the requirement for a specific injunction, a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) is inferred; therefore, the expectation is equal regarding both the object to be enjoined and the object to be excluded. (2.353)
There is no elision of that which is a part of a name-word; that name, having been formed with its specific form, does not cease to exist. (2.354)
Furthermore, no name other than "Datta" and the like is perceived; how then could the word "Datta" denote the named object known as Devadatta? (2.355)

Some maintain that the individual word-forms have a connection with all their constituent parts that is equal to the connection they have with the entire aggregate, just as they do with all the things named by them. (2.356)
The meaningfulness of phonemes occurs through their relationship with the things they name; a related constituent part cannot be conceived in the absence of a distinct name. (2.357)

When there is a simultaneous connection with all the individual forms of the named object, it is impossible for that object to be conveyed by means of those [forms] which resemble it only in part. (2.358)
However, from a single part [of the whole], memory arises for some regarding the aggregate;
and from the word, which is the object of that memory, the meaning of the aggregate is understood. (2.359)
How could memory be restricted to a specific part within a distinct aggregate?
And how could a word, being perceived [as such], be the designator of an object? (2.360)
But words that share a common form in part, yet are endowed with various specific distinctions, exist as designations established through their secondary production. (2.361)
Because they are common [to all], they are ambiguous; yet by virtue of their functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), they have fixed substrata.
Among those [words], for those that are correct, rules such as elision (*lopa*) and so forth are taught in the treatise. (2.362)
When the co-occurrence [of suffixes] is equal, forms such as *jyeṣṭhāghā* are incorrect;
for there is no traditional authority (*smṛti*) for them in the explanatory grammatical treatise, as there is for words like *datta*. (2.363)
And those words that have been established as eternal, such as *kharaṇasa* and others, are declared to be correct because they are taught to denote a single substance. (2.364)

But they say that these are indeed *gotras* (lineages/species), because they possess the capacity for designation; it is not necessarily required that they depend on external causes for their own meaning. (2.365)

The restriction of names to a named object is for the sake of conventional usage; however, the relationship in the case of "Dittha" and so forth is indeed eternal, just like that between a cow and its name.
Because it is produced, the impermanence of the relationship is established; for in the case of a name, it is applied by persons according to their own will. (2.367)
For just as names such as "sweet" and so forth are applied by children to lines drawn in the sand, this very same conceptual construction applies to all designations. (2.368)

Moreover, in this treatise, the relationship between [the concepts of] increase and so forth is indeed non-artificial, characterized by the delimitation of capacities, just like that between a qualifier and a qualificand. (2.369)
Depending on its own essential nature, worldly conceptualization (saṃjñā) occurs when a causal sign (nimitta) is present; some [conceptualizations] occur even in the absence of a causal sign. (2.370)
In the treatise as well, the great designation is based upon the essential nature [of the object];
inference is recognized when the cause is present. (2.371)
In that case, inference is understood either from repetition due to similarity, or as an inference from the difference in words, or as the comprehension of a difference in capacity. (2.372)
In some cases, artificial [distinctions] are established through a difference in objects;
however, regarding number, the establishment of a single object applies to both as well. (2.373)

Even when uttered in some cases by a worldly person, a word reaches its object even from afar; for indeed, in the case of perfect cognition, there is a grasping of both [the word and the object]. (2.374)

Regarding the cases of the community (saṅgha), the remainder (ekaśeṣa), and the dual (dvandva), some maintain that actions reside in each respective substratum by virtue of their functional capacity. (2.375)
The meal is completed in each [instance] by means of both the fruit and the form;
for otherwise, in such an arrangement, its purpose would not be fulfilled. (2.376)
And all individuals experience the act of eating—in the form of taking food and so forth—as resulting in the fruit of individual satisfaction, but not as if it were a theatrical performance. (2.377)

Like water for the feet, it remains distinct according to its capacity; the root *bhuj* performs the action for the sake of the object of enjoyment, not by a single simultaneous application (*tantra*), as in the case of a lamp. (2.378)
But even a single action such as "seeing" may, when applied to such objects of action, pertain to a collection [of instances] even without repetition. (2.379)

When one observes activities such as worldly transactions performed by agents whose forms and functions are distinct, the observation of these distinct agents establishes the accomplishment of a single purpose through their collective action. (2.380)

Because the object to be characterized is established by common worldly usage, and because the indicative mark is seen in the treatise, the designation "vṛddhi" is completed by distinguishing [the vowels] among those seeking the goal, beginning with *ā*. (2.381)

Because the primary element is the taking of a hundred, even when the punishment consists of a hundred acts, the object to be counted does not differ among claimants, despite differences in their specific qualities. (2.382)

Because it must be carried out by the Saṅgha alone, like a formal duty, the connection there is by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application) regarding the technical designations of *samāsa* and *abhyasta*. (2.383)
For those for whom scripture has the purpose of defining [the means] toward some particular action, that Dharma is characterized by them, both individually and collectively. (2.384)
Just as in the case of this house where it is said, "Śūdras must not enter," the entry of both those who are gathered together and those who are individual is prohibited. (2.385)

However, when there is instruction regarding the prohibition of the desire for gain and so forth through collective action, activity is not contradicted because such [individual] activity is not prohibited separately. (2.386)

Because the purpose [of the rule] is to define the scope of *vyavāya* (separation), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is not prohibited by the presence of *aṭ*, *k*, *p*, *v*, *āṅ*, and so forth—whether these occur individually or collectively. (2.387)
When the act of eating is undertaken for the sake of favoring those who eat, yet it does not favor them due to differences in place, time, and so forth—[then there is no fault]. (2.388)
The multiplicity of a single entity is taught on account of the differences in its vessels and so forth; or conversely, the unity of that which is divided is conceptually constructed. (2.389)
Even when acting in combination, they are presented as distinct;
having each obtained their own respective food, they enjoy it together through division. (2.390)

Because there is no scope for repetition (*vīpsā*), because of contradiction with another number, and because completion in two ways is impossible, the number "one hundred" remains fixed upon the assembly (*saṅgha*). (2.391)

Where a single remainder is taught through either a *dvandva* or a *ekaśeṣa* compound together with other [words], even there the sentence is completed in two ways because of the purpose of indicating the characteristics [of the elements]. (2.392)
Some maintain that each of the other sentences has its own completion; by this [definition], there is an inclusion of those sentences joined with different forms. (2.393)
There are no distinct sentences that constitute the denotata of a sentence; rather, when that [sentence] is uttered, one likewise apprehends various distinctions within it. (2.394)
For those for whom the entire meaning of a sentence is completed at each individual word, what purpose would there be at that time for the existence of a distinct word-meaning? (2.395)
Or, if that object produced by those very [causes] exists within distinct [moments], then there would either be a contradiction with the previous object or a coexistence with it. (2.396)
If they coexist, there would be a contradiction between the qualified and the unqualified;
however, if the object is abandoned, the relationship becomes inconstant. (2.397)
The single, common denotable essence resides in each individual word; it is the self-nature of the meaning within the collection and its members, acting as the indicator of their presence. (2.398)
Just as ownership of wealth is common [to all] and the fruit of its relinquishment is equal joy, so too is the connection with that object for those who possess it. (2.399)
When the phonemes possess meaning, that very meaning does not reside in the collection as a single unity, since it remains established through its distinctness. (2.400)
Just as all people see common property by means of a single lamp, in the same way, number is designated by means of a single excellence (sup). 2.401.
Thus, meaningfulness is not distinguished [as being present] in the word, the phoneme, or the sentence;
rather, through repetition, a different sequence appears as if it were contradictory. (2.402)

Apart from its application (viniyoga), a word does not reveal its own meaning; they declare that the connection for the expression of meaning is mediated by the statement [of that application]. (2.403)
Just as the eye, when directed, serves for the purpose of seeing, so too a word, when intended, becomes the designator of an object. (2.404)
A connection between the instrument and the object is observed to be mediated by an action;
therefore, there is a restriction of expression between the signifier and the signified. (2.405)
When many things are denoted by a single name and all of them perform the same function, the word remains fixed upon that which the speaker intends. (2.406)
Some say that the words of the sacred tradition are meaningless when used in repetition, while others hold that they function solely to convey their own formal nature to others. (2.407)

Those who perceive [the Veda] as a single entity consider the various injunctions (*niyoga*)—which bring about the understanding of an object through their connection with the act of denotation—to be nothing other than those very [injunctions]. (2.408)

Those who employ conventional designations for diversity declare that there is absolute non-difference among them, because they are connected with a single genus, just as in the case of the sense organs and so forth. (2.409)
In these cases, no intention other than the actual application is found;
for since he acts according to his capacity regarding the object, he is established therein. (2.410)
The cognition of diversity itself [arises] from the context of the meaning and other factors; how indeed could words denoting one object ever function with reference to a different object? (2.411)

And as for that sentence which consists of words and is bound up with existence, let this investigation apply to it at will; it does not apply to a word, which is a constituent part of a sentence. (2.412)
Just as a specific meaning is expressed by means of meaningless phonemes, so too is a specific meaning expressed by means of meaningless words. (2.413)

The cognition that arises with respect to objects in the interval [between the initial perception and the final ascertainment] is a means to comprehension, because the final conclusion has not yet been determined through the process of inquiry. (2.414)
Just as the ultimate nature of reality is followed by preceding meanings, so too does association itself proceed among other objective entities. (2.415)
But when some means of proof have already been accepted as proving a certain probandum, the restatement of those means of proof serves solely to restrict their substratum. (2.416)

Since there is no restrictive rule regarding the substratum, there is no implication of it; its possibility arises from the force of the context, while the explicit mention serves to exclude anything else. (2.417)
An action is distinct from other actions and possesses a fixed substratum and means;
it is undertaken by practitioners, and its various distinctions are the causes for full awakening. (2.418)
But for others, that sentence and its meaning appear as indivisible from the words, even though the words possess a sequence; thus it appears without a sequential order of words. (2.419)
The self of that which possesses an intrinsic nature cannot be defined;
however, the self of that which lacks an intrinsic nature is indeed defined. (2.420)
Others know that the determination of an object's form is wordless;
and memory, which has the appearance of the object, arises from words. (2.421)
In one way, one who is burned perceives the burning through contact with fire;
in another way, the meaning of "burning" is understood by means of the word "burning. (2.422)
Just as for the sense faculties—which are established separately and follow their respective objects—no activity is possible apart from the body. (2.423)
Likewise, for all words that are established as having individual meanings, once they are separated from sentences, their possessors of meaning are not found to exist. (2.424)
The nature of conjunction is perceived in objects that are conjoined;
however, the true reality [of the self] is not described here, because it is seen to be not an object [of the senses]. (2.425)
Even that which is the truth of perception does not exist as perception;
for an object, when characterized by its association with other forms, is determined to be formless. (2.426)
Since an object is expressed as being either connected with existence or as residing within its own nature, therefore a sentence is employed. (2.427)
Without connection to an action, an object is not cognized;
whether it be real or otherwise, such an [independent] entity does not exist in practical discourse. (2.428)
But this sentence "it is existent" (sad iti) is understood as either "it was" or "it exists," and it cannot be comprehended without a connection to the expression of an action. (2.429)
When the meaning expressed by a verb is connected with its means of accomplishment (sādhana), the expectancy [of the sentence] does not cease without the expression of a substance (sattva). (2.430)
However, because of its predominance, action is analyzed first; the constituent parts are employed for the sake of what is to be accomplished, and the fruit is the motivator of that [action]. (2.431)
The speaker alone intends the nature of the goal and the means, and he likewise strives for the conceptualization of the connection between the objects. (2.432)

That which "performs the act of cooking" is designated as the object (*karman*); however, the "cooking" itself, in its form as an instrument (*karaṇa*), is perceived as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). (2.433)
Whatever aspect of an object is intended by the speakers through whatever means of assistance, that aspect remains established exactly in that way, because the object possesses all powers. (2.434)
In the case of remote functions, a relation is sometimes expressed;
that which is embraced [by the function] but not directly contiguous is sometimes perceived. (2.435)
The state of being divided belongs to those who are united, and union belongs to those who are discerning;
unity belongs to things of diverse nature, and diversity occurs in the opposite case. (2.436)
Because an object is either identical with all things or devoid of self-nature, it is established that only the word is the basis [of its cognition], since its power is absolutely restricted. (2.437)
A word that merely characterizes an object does not express a benefit;
therefore, it is not possible for it to touch upon the inherent power of things. (2.438)

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is a property of related things, is denoted by its own specific term; however, inherence (*samavāya*), as a relation, is understood only through the fact of being related. (2.439)
Objects are established by way of their defining characteristics, but not in reality;
that very object is understood in some manner through its functional utility. (2.440)
The meaning of a sentence is the connection [between word-meanings]; its essence does not reside anywhere [independently].
In linguistic usage, they designate that very essence as the "meaning of the words. (2.441)
Whether it be completed in a single word-meaning or in a collection of them, its nature is never divided anywhere according to the distinctions in the forms of those word-meanings. (2.442)

The distinction that serves as the basis for comprehension in order to provide a grammatical exposition is described as something else; by means of that distinction, the whole is characterized as having parts that are mutually expectant. (2.443)
The differentiation of the many powers of a single [word] is observed; for the unity of meaning of a sentence is indeed perceived even by a slight degree. (2.444)
An external object, whether existent or non-existent, is distinguished for the sake of conceptual determination;
however, this distinction made by treating it as external is characterized by the abstraction of its potencies. (2.445)
The powers, restricted to their own respective objects and conditions, are not fixed;
nor is their form perceived elsewhere than in those [objects]. (2.446)
Even when there are many finite verbs (tiṅanta) that are mutually expectant, they constitute a single sentence;
thus, the prohibition of the suppression of accent (nighāta) by one finite verb [before] others becomes meaningful. (2.447)

For one for whom a sentence is defined in the treatise as having exactly one finite verb (tiṅ), there is no need for the mention of "non-finite" (atiṅ) [in the definition], because no such distinction of sentences exists. (2.448)

Furthermore, when joined with other verbs ending in verbal suffixes (tiṅanta), or even when joined with words already connected [to another verb], as in "Look, the deer is going," neither distinction nor non-distinction remains. (2.449)
Where the sense of what must be done is expected through the force of the context, yet lacks a verbal indicator for that expectation, that is said to be a completed meaning. (2.450)
But in the case of a mere restatement of a fact, whatever purpose follows as a consequence is fulfilled by the Vedic revelation itself;
even without the employment of that [subsequent statement], the sentence reaches its completion through the scripture. (2.451)
"Study while walking; perform the recitation while walking.
Although there is no difference in their purpose, a distinction is perceived from the words themselves. (2.452)
The various actions that bear fruit are dependent upon other actions; though they are innumerable and indicated by sequential descriptions, they are all shown within a single verbal root. (2.453)
In a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), every action is expressed as entirely devoid of internal differentiation;
it is impossible for the scripture to conceive of a division among these differentiations. (2.454)
"Kings will sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice; Brahmins are performing a long sacrificial session"—from such expressions, no distinction [between the two classes] is perceived. (2.455)
The ritual action which is heard once within the seventeen [offerings] and is not repeated, attains differentiation by virtue of its capacity within the Prājāpatya offerings. (2.456)
In cases such as "Devadatta and others," the verb *bhuji* (to eat) resides with each [individual] separately;
or rather, it is understood as distinct sentences, each possessing its own independence. (2.457)
Upon the utterance of sentences, no other form is perceived;
yet upon their comprehension, a different form is understood for those [sentences] that appear distinct. (2.458)

A single statement of enunciation is expressed in general terms, such as "by the agent"; and that [general rule] is then divided among specific instances, such as sacrificial animals and the like. (2.459)
If the expectancy were to cease upon the single hearing of that which has come into being, how could it not fail to enter into a connection with anything else? (2.460)
It is of a single form yet possesses manifold meanings; therefore, it is the basis [of expression], the source of analytical statements, existing as if non-different from them. (2.461)
In some cases, the action proceeds toward assistance by means of its individualized parts; in other cases, it is the universal aspect alone that accomplishes the purpose. (2.462)
The word-soul is not divided by those distinctions that differ in time, nor by those such as "the camel-sitting" and so forth, which occur when a portion of a genus is being introduced. (2.463)
Among the various individual instances numbered as one, actions differentiated by genus and other factors are employed separately when that word is heard only once. (2.464)

Just as in the case of [the roots] *akṣ* and so forth, the distinct actions of eating (*bhakṣi*), breaking (*bhañji*), and playing (*divi*) remain separate for each individual action, even though there is no difference in the time of their application. (2.465)
The "string" of the strings [of the senses] is the means, which is their uniformity; the "sequence" of these when divided is their simultaneous perception as bound together by that [means]. (2.466)
Two methods for the employment of words are established: either succession or simultaneity, which the world does not transcend. (2.467)
Form is divided when there is succession, but it is not differentiated when there is simultaneity;
however, action, even in the case of simultaneity, follows the form of succession. (2.468)

The two powers of differentiation and connection remain as if distinct from the word; even when they occur simultaneously, the auditory perception is differentiated by their manifold application. (2.469)
When a single entity intended to be expressed is not differentiated by its various forms, the whole is understood through the properties of its parts. (2.470)

Regarding the definition of its division, however, the verbal expression either terminates with each individual [element], or it remains distinct in its utterance when there is a division of the sentence. (2.471)
In that case, either that word *akṣa* is used in the singular number, or it is divided into a plurality for each [organ] according to the literal expression. (2.472)

Even in those statements which appear to reside in two [entities], for those who perceive their unity, the inherent power of a single entity possessing manifold capacities is divided [into parts]. (2.473)

Or rather, when two things are absolutely distinct, the means [of cognition] would have the characteristic of being common (tantra) in its application; in that case, the connection [between them] differs according to the cognizers. (2.474)
Having previously understood two words of identical sound as distinct, the listeners are now led by the speaker to comprehend them simultaneously through a single effort. (2.475)
Even when only one [meaning] is intended to be expressed, the other follows along;
the word, manifesting in the form of a power (*śakti*), shines forth even without a deliberate intention [to express it]. (2.476)
In some cases, multiple powers of a single entity are heard of as occurring simultaneously; for example, fire is employed for both illumination and burning even in a single instance. (2.477)

Even when a sentence whose meaning is differentiated by the power of repetition is heard only once, the distinction [between its parts] is established either through indicative mark (liṅga) or through the principle of common application (tantra). (2.478)
In the definition of *saṃprasāraṇa*, a distinction between a phoneme and a sentence arises through two indicators, even within a single sūtra. (2.479)

Likewise, regarding the doubling [of a consonant] by the rule *aco ra ṛti* (P. 8.4.46), the indication is shown in the Bhāṣya itself to be without a formal marker (*alakṣaṇa*) through the method of ellipsis (*tantra*), by means of a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*). (2.480)
Generally, when the *Saṃgraha* had disappeared, grammarians were encountered who took pleasure in brevity and possessed only a limited grasp of knowledge. (2.481)
Then, when the teacher Patañjali, the seer of the sacred truths, had composed the *Mahābhāṣya*, which is the compendium of all the seeds of logic. (2.482)
Because its depth has not been fathomed due to its profundity, and because it appears superficial due to its elegance, those of untrained intellect have established no certainty regarding it. (2.483)
When the treatise of the Ṛṣi, which was merely a compilation serving as a patchwork, had been corrupted by the Vaiśeṣikas, Saubhavas, and Haryakṣas who followed dry logic, [it was restored]. (2.484)
The tradition of grammar that had fallen away from the disciples of Patañjali remained, over time, among those of the South as nothing more than the written text. (2.485)
Having received the tradition from Parvata, it was further expanded into many branches by Cāndrācārya and others who followed the seeds of the Bhāṣya.
Having studied those systems of the path of logic as well as our own philosophical view, this compendium of scripture has been composed for us by our teacher. (2.487)
In this [chapter], only the mere substance of certain paths has been illustrated; a detailed investigation will take place in the third section (kāṇḍa). (2.488)
Wisdom attains discernment through the various perspectives of the scriptures; for how much can be raised by one who merely follows his own reasoning? (2.489)
For those who speculate on this and that without the ancient scriptures and who have not served their elders, knowledge does not become fully clear. (2.490)
Thus ends the Vākyakāṇḍa in the Vākyapadīya composed by Bhartṛhari.
3. Section on Words (Padakāṇḍa) 3.1. Exposition of Genus (Jātisamuddeśa):
By some, the word is divided in two ways; by others, in four ways, or even in five ways.
Or rather, it is extracted from sentences, just like the base and suffixes [are extracted] from words. (3.1.1)
When the meanings of words are abstracted, it is described that for all words, the referents are either the universal (jāti) or the substance (dravya), both of which are indeed eternal. (3.1.2)

In some cases, the genus serves as an indicator of capacity by virtue of association; when the *khadira* and other such trees lack the capacity, one that possesses the capacity is substituted for them. (3.1.3)
Bondage, which has lack of independence as its fruit, remains [as a reality] just like the means of valid cognition and so forth;
therefore, even when a genus is denoted, that which is devoid of causal capacity is not apprehended. (3.1.4)

If what is intended [by the root *bandh*] is merely "to connect," then gender (*liṅga*) is the locus of capacity; thus, the instruction regarding [the three] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth [is established]. (3.1.5)
One's own genus is expressed first by all words;
thereafter, there arises the conceptual construction of superimposing that [genus] upon the forms of the object-genuses. (3.1.6)
Just as the reality of the quality "red" is designated in the dye, and due to contact with that which possesses it, it is also perceived in garments and other objects; (3.1.7)

Likewise, through the relationship between word and object, the universal (jāti) resides in the word; it serves to effect the function of the universal for the objects denoted when they are designated. (3.1.8)

In the case of a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) of genus-words (*jātiśabda*), that [genus] is intended as the genus of those genera; for instance, in the expression "classes of words" (*śabdajātayaḥ*), that genus [of wordhood] resides within the classes of words. (3.1.9)
That universal which, among words denoting word-universals, possesses a characteristic distinct from [individual] words, exists without deviating from its status as a word-universal. (3.1.10)

Even when there is the denotation of a meaning as a universal (jāti), all [words] denote universals, because word-meanings are established as being characterized by functional activity (vyāpāra). (3.1.11)
Since, in the case of an entity that is a genus, either the genus or a particularity is expected by words just like a genus, therefore those [words] are denoters of the genus. (3.1.12)
In the case of a category (padārtha), however, every object is said to possess the properties of substance when it is a substance;
because it is the locus of the properties of substance, therefore every object is accepted as being a substance. (3.1.13)
Alternatively, "birth" (jāti) might be a property of persistence across all classes;
however, it is accepted that a universal characterized by exclusion [from others] constitutes birth within a particular class. (3.1.14)
When space is conceptually constructed as a location through the distinction of properties associated with conjunction, the universal of space exists within those locations as well. (3.1.15)

Just as objects such as pots, which lack spatial location, have locations that are their relations, so too does space, though itself without location, have locations in the form of its conjuncts. (3.1.16)
Cognition based on distinct objects persists among things that are conjoined;
however, among things that are inherent, the apprehension of distinction ceases. (3.1.17)

Therefore, the status of being secondary is attributed to the locations of the conjoined [substances], while the status of being primary belongs to the inherent [substances] because they cannot be distinguished from those locations. (3.1.18)

Some know that *ākṛti* (form) is the manifestation whose nature is conformity (*anupravṛtti*); however, others describe it as being of the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and as substance (*dravya*). (3.1.19)
"Distinct" or "indistinct"—this conceptual proliferation regarding the nature of entities arises only when they are in conjunction with external conditions. (3.1.20)
Neither unity nor multiplicity, neither existence nor non-existence, is found in the true nature of things, which are entirely unconditioned. (3.1.21)
If it is determined that the state of being the self of all powers belongs to one alone, then the postulation of a difference in the natures of entities would be purposeless. (3.1.22)
Therefore, all powers such as substance and the rest, which possess distinct characteristics, accomplish the purpose of the person when combined, but not when isolated. (3.1.23)

Just as the completeness of the sense organs and so forth is itself the self-nature [of their functioning], so too is it perceived in the connection between related things and in their mutual association. (3.1.24)
Nothing whatsoever arises for which birth does not exist;
birth is the motivator of causes for the manifestation of the self. (3.1.25)
Having established their footing among causes—both eternal and non-eternal—these generic types repeatedly attain manifestation in certain effects. (3.1.26)
Even in the case of an object (*karman*) that is being produced (*nirvartyamāna*), the genus (*jāti*) is the means (*sādhana*);
it is that [genus] which instigates the action for the sake of bringing about its own substratum. 3.1.27.

Whether in an injunction or in a prohibition, the means of proof [for caste] such as Brahminhood and so forth is the universal of number, which resides in the individual and is itself resorted to by the universal of genus; it serves as its qualifier. (3.1.28)
Just as the face itself is designated when it is manifested by water and so forth, so too the universal (jāti) itself is designated when it is manifested by substances. (3.1.29)

Just as a distinction residing in the sense organ serves to differentiate cognitions even without being perceived itself, so too [a distinction] among the objects of the senses, though invisible, serves to differentiate cognitions. (3.1.30)
Likewise, for some individuals who grasp the form of the self, even without [perceiving] particulars, universals become the cause for the distinctions of cognitions. (3.1.31)
In every individual entity, there exist two parts: the real and the unreal.
That which is real therein is the universal (jāti); the individuals (vyakti) are considered to be unreal. (3.1.32)
Being itself, when differentiated according to its various relata in cows and other things, is called "universal" (jāti); all words are established in that [Being]. (3.1.33)
They declare that to be the meaning of the nominal stem and the meaning of the verbal root;
it is eternal, it is the Great Self, and they call it the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and so forth. (3.1.34)
That very same activity, when occurring in a sequence among particulars, is designated as "action" (kriyā);
when the form of that sequence is withdrawn, it is called "pure being" (sattva). (3.1.35)
That very [consciousness], undergoing modifications of state, attains six conditions;
thus it manifests itself sequentially through its own powers. (3.1.36)
Even the sequence inherent in this [consciousness], wherein this perception of time exists, stands as if divided into forms such as priority and posteriority. (3.1.37)
When the concealment of entities is admitted, that very state is their non-existence; once concealment has attained its sequence, it is perceived as "perishing. (3.1.38)

Having fallen away from the previous dharma and not yet having attained the higher state, birth is said to occur in the interval between those two due to the reliance upon various distinctions. (3.1.39)
The causes for the perception of difference in "Being" (sattā) are either its own substratum alone, or entities distinct from it, or its own inherent powers (śakti). (3.1.40)
In the case of manifestation in earth and the other elements, it does not depend on a specific configuration;
for a genus, because its substratum is never severed, remains even when that substratum is impermanent. (3.1.41)
Some declare that every birth has an indestructible substratum;
they maintain that there is no simultaneous dissolution of everything at once. (3.1.42)

When the particulars have dissolved back into their primordial nature (prakṛti), the universals (jātis), which perceive unity, attain the state of substantial existence (dravyasattva) within their own respective substrates. (3.1.43)
The states such as being a Brahmin and so forth reside in all living beings;
they are manifested and serve to accomplish their respective functions—thus also says the Smṛti. (3.1.44)
Some maintain that even in paintings and the like, there is a manifestation of universal classes (jāti);
however, those [classes] residing in living beings serve as the cause for merit and demerit upon their acquisition. (3.1.45)

But those who are superior to us know that, through practice, all-sensory cognition arises regarding those [subtle objects], just as it does for experts concerning the specific qualities of gems, silver, and so forth. (3.1.46)

In the world, that reality of difference which is dependent upon the fragrance of the *jāti* lily and so forth is not denoted by abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) because of its impermanence. (3.1.47)

But for the classes such as "Man-Lion" (narasiṃha), which are denoted by words that do not signify their constituent parts, another auditory perception remains established in them, as if their parts possessed similar forms. (3.1.48)
In the determination of the state of a universal, number—or even the very nature of number—contributes to its assistance through association, even when it is remote. (3.1.49)

The function of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is observed in the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words for the sake of accomplishing the intended effect; this occurs even when the verbal roots are identical, as in the case of the powers of number, object, and so forth. (3.1.50)
No entity existing as a sentient being is ever denoted without a number; therefore, in the description of every such thing, the number would be unintended [as a significant qualifier]. (3.1.51)
For some, unity or plurality is not intended to be expressed;
indeed, that [unity] is for the purpose of denoting the genus, whereas duality would be intended to be expressed. (3.1.52)
"If these two were diseased, this medicine should be given"—in such a case, the duality of the object [the patients] would be unintended [by the speaker]. (3.1.53)

The number expressed by words such as "one" and so forth is accepted as being subsidiary to the ritual actions; for it is dependent [on the verb] due to its form, as in the examples "he digs" and "with two. (3.1.54)

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal," just as the genus [of the animal] is understood as the means of accomplishment, so too is its singularity understood as a means, since even a preparatory rite (saṃskāra) is possible therein. (3.1.55)
But from the grammatical gender (liṅga), there may be the second [dual] and so on; therefore, that singularity is intended to be expressed.
And when they have a single object as their domain, that gender [and number] belong to both the genus and the number. (3.1.56)
That [act] is first a rule for the animal sacrifice itself when it has not been prescribed elsewhere;
moreover, its status as a subordinate member (aṅga) in the ritual action is what is intended to be expressed by this [sūtra]. (3.1.57)
But elsewhere, the planets are prescribed with various distinct numbers, endowed with such distinctions as "nine for Prajāpati" and so forth. (3.1.58)

When those understood as subordinate members (aṅga) are indeed being purified, how could the number mentioned in relation to the instruction of the principal members (aṅgin) be intended [to apply to the purification]? (3.1.59)

There is no injunction elsewhere, nor is there a refinement (saṃskāra), nor even the status of being a primary factor (aṅgitā); for the intention to express a number is a cause [of its application], since it is indeed intended through deliberate effort. (3.1.60)

Furthermore, no specific [rule] regarding the sweeping is based on the cup (graha) anywhere; rather, those [sweepings] have been prescribed as purificatory acts (saṃskāra), and therefore they are the substratum for all [the cups]. (3.1.61)

If, when the birth [of the sacrificial animal] has been completed for each individual substratum, the ritual action were not to be performed with even a single animal, then that very performance would indeed be possible. (3.1.62)

And if, when one [animal] is established for the performance of the rite, another animal could be substituted because it is possible [to do so], then the specific injunction regarding the material would be purposeless. (3.1.63)

Just as the rite of impregnation (garbhādhāna) is useless for a woman who is already pregnant, so too is another animal sacrifice useless when [the result] has already been accomplished by one. (3.1.64)

Some maintain that because the purpose is accomplished by that much alone, there should be no deviation from the singular number; however, in this case, the number is not taken as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) of the action. (3.1.65)
But whatever gender is expressed from the second case onwards merely restates the previously stated rule; it is not understood as a means [of accomplishment], just like a genus (jāti). (3.1.66)

When number is accepted on the basis of positive and negative concomitance, it is logical that it should function as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and not as a mere indicator of another object. (3.1.67)
When a word-meaning functions as a means [to an action], its capacity is not lost;
therefore, by that very mark, the property of the operation of number is understood. (3.1.68)

Because that which is not previously established is what is to be enjoined, its primacy is determined; because that which has been enjoined exists for the sake of another, its status as a subordinate element is understood. (3.1.69)

Since the sweeping is that which is to be enjoined, when the cup (graha) has been enjoined elsewhere, the number heard in the injunctive sentence is not sublated by the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). (3.1.70)
In another injunctive sentence, there is no number that contradicts the singularity of the animal;
therefore, it is understood as possessing that quality together with oneness. (3.1.71)

When a substance has already been ascertained through its connection [with another], that quality which is prescribed in relation to the action is understood to have a requirement for that substance, just as the substance itself does. (3.1.72)
Just as a certain quality in a substance is characterized by its capacity (sāmarthya), so too the substratum of that very quality is established as being characterized by capacity. (3.1.73)

But when those two are sought as distinct entities, the relationship that is perceived between them is not impaired; nor is it necessary to postulate anything else that is not heard in the text. (3.1.74)

The connection between those two—the substratum and the superstratum—is established by direct audition (śruti) through the action; however, the restriction [of their specific application] is determined by the sentence (vākya). (3.1.75)

In that case, in the absence of a substance and a quality, there would be an option for each [word], because the connection established by direct audition (śruti) is stronger than that characterized by syntactical connection (vākya). (3.1.76)

But when either a genus or a capacity is taught with reference to an action, then, by virtue of contextual implication (*sāmarthya*), the substance and the quality are brought into proximity there. (3.1.77)
When the genus (*jāti*) and the qualities (*guṇa*) are equally auxiliary to the ritual action, the qualities of the goat and other animals may be substituted, but not their genera. (3.1.78)
Genera are closer to the individual power [of manifestation] than qualities are;
substance is directly connected with action, whereas a quality is differentiated from it. (3.1.79)
Some maintain that when there is an absence of either [alternative] due to parity, there is an option;
therefore, the goat would not possess those qualities, or the ram would possess them. (3.1.80)
The occurrence of a number inherent in a genus is observed;
sometimes that very same [number] occurs while setting aside a specific number. (3.1.81)
A genus that has become a subordinate element (parāṅga) is connected with the number of the substance;
however, when it functions toward its own primary meaning (svārtha), it does not depend upon number. (3.1.82)

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal," when the word "animal" is heard as being for the purpose of the sacrifice, the primary action is accomplished by means of that single animal. (3.1.83)

If one were to perform the touching (*ālambhana*) of as many [animals] as are available, then by that [act], the primary [sacrifice] would be rendered effective through its constituent qualities (*guṇa*). (3.1.84)
But where there is a scriptural injunction for an action regarding a vessel used in a ritual context that involves cleansing, we do not take any account of the mention of a specific number. (3.1.85)

The fact that the word "one" (eka) was employed in the rule concerning the remaining part of the sentence (*śiṣyamāṇapara-vākya*) is clearly an indicator (*liṅga*) [of this principle], even though the remainder possesses a specific number. (3.1.86)

Just as the Vedic revelation, when it occurs in the formulation of compound words and suffixes, is logically established according to the principle that subordinate factors are dependent upon others. (3.1.87)

Even though it is a quality (*guṇa*), number is not accepted as being for the sake of establishing another primary element (*pradhāna*); likewise, the agent is understood as being non-distinct from the object. (3.1.88)
When there is another [element] that might be expected to apply, the repetition of the rule is for the purpose of restriction;
however, the case-ending which is prescribed after a collection of similar forms [is governed by this rule]. (Pāṇini 1.4.102)
Since its purpose has been fulfilled upon the completion [of the action], the number is not intended to be significant there;
thus, one [element] is established as meaningful, serving as the designator of the aggregate. (3.1.90)

Whether in the prescription of a suffix (*pratyaya*), a primary element (*pradhāna*), or even a compound (*samāsa*), when the expression of number is intended, the subordinate element (*guṇa*) is in every respect subject to the inclusion [of its gender and number]. (3.1.91)
Similarity is of the nature of non-difference, and the powers are identical with the self;
it is further described that these [powers] are also denotable by synonyms for the universal (jāti).
Even if one acquires a staff with the desire to take up a staff, one is not perceived as "staff-bearer" solely on the basis of that [act of acquisition]. (3.1.93)
The cognition "one who has desire" does not arise from the cause that is the desire itself;
therefore, even when the capacity [to produce it] exists, the intellect (buddhi) rests upon something other than the object [itself]. (3.1.94)
In the end, everything rests either upon an ineffable intrinsic nature or upon causal capacity; therefore, conventional linguistic usage is not ultimately tenable.

When, having set aside the differences, it is grasped by the intellect as if it were one, then the intellect operates as a single unity directed toward the very nature of the individual manifestation itself. (3.1.96)
When the intellect perceives that which is permeated by diverse forms as if it were one, then that cognition arises from many [objects] through the grasping of a collection. (3.1.97)

When there is a desire to express [the parts] together, a collection whose constituent parts are bound together by a single cognition is denoted as a whole, with its internal divisions set aside. (3.1.98)

Because the counter-action is completed, it is endowed with a single division; however, in a copulative compound (dvandva), it is understood as such through the distinction of duality and so forth. (3.1.99)

Through the exclusion of difference (*bhedāpoha*), individuals that possess distinct natures attain oneness when they occur simultaneously, and they attain a state of similarity when they recur. (3.1.100)
"Just as a cognition is perceived as distinct when it follows [the object], so too is the object grasped in its true nature, even though its form is differentiated. (3.1.101)
For all things that possess identical forms, there exist no denotative words that do not involve some distinction; nor is any such distinction perceived. (3.1.102)
Because those specific distinctions established as the objects of knowledge, words, and meanings are difficult to discern, there is the perception of the identity of knowledge and the rest. (3.1.103)
Likewise, even in all cognitions that correspond to reality, there exist universals (*jāti*) within the perception of relations; and these [universals] are what establish the object.
The universal residing only within the object of cognition is what assists cognitions;
for a cognition is never manifested by the form of another, just as the object itself is not. (3.1.105)
Just as light is not illuminated by another light, so the form of cognition is not grasped by another cognition. (3.1.106)
Furthermore, the power of cognition would not be capable of determining a universal inherent in the self, if another object were already known [by that same cognition]. (3.1.107)

If cognitions do not occur simultaneously, there would be no apprehension of "this" [the object]; furthermore, recollection arises only with respect to what has been perceived, in accordance with that perception. (3.1.108)
The cognition "the cognition of a jar" is distinct from the cognition of the jar itself; whereas the cognition "jar," which occurs in relation to its object, is that [latter]. (3.1.109)
Because the form of cognition is not grasped as having the form of the object, and its own nature is not determined as distinct from the form of the object. (3.1.110)
Thus concludes the summary of the categories.
3.2 Summary of Substance (Dravyasamuddeśa) Self, entity, intrinsic nature, body, and reality—
these are synonyms for "substance" (dravya), and it is traditionally held that it is eternal. (3.2.1)
The real object is determined by means of unreal forms;
the Real itself is expressed by words that possess unreal adjuncts. (3.2.2)
Just as Devadatta’s house, though apprehended by means of an impermanent cause, is denoted by the word "house" as being purely [the house itself], so too is it expressed. (3.2.3)
Just as gold and other substances, when joined with their own non-permanent forms, come to be designated by such names as "necklace" and so forth, yet remain pure [in essence]. (3.2.4)

And because it is delimited by specific modes [of activity], its universal capacity is restricted, just as the capacity of the eyes and other organs is restricted by conditions such as blindness. (3.2.5)
The word that functions with respect to those forms as they truly are, because it consists of their very essence, denotes them as eternally so. (3.2.6)
"There is no distinction between reality and unreality"—this is the traditional teaching from the elders.
They consider that which is called "unreality" to be simply reality itself when left unexamined. (3.2.7)
The reality itself, though free from conceptual construction, assumes the form of conceptual construction;
yet there is no difference in time here, even though a difference in time is perceived.

Just as the properties of objects are absolutely impossible within cognition, so too is that [cognition] established as being absolutely not of the nature of those [objects], even though it appears as if it were their very self. (3.2.9)

Likewise, there is an absolute impossibility of the forms of modifications existing within reality; and that reality, though appearing as if it were their very self, is in fact absolutely not of their nature. (3.2.10)
That which remains at the end when the withdrawal of forms has occurred is eternal; it is denotable by words, it is expressed by words, and it is not distinct from those words. (3.2.11)
It is not that it exists, nor is it that it does not exist; it is not one, nor is it separate;
it is neither conjoined nor divided, neither transformed nor otherwise. (3.2.12)
That does not exist, yet it exists; it is one, yet it is manifold; it is conjoined and it is divided; it is transformed, and it is otherwise. (3.2.13)
Of that [cognition], the nature of the relationship between word and object is seen as one;
that which is seen, the seeing, the seer, and the purpose of the seeing [are all observed therein]. (3.2.14)
Just as gold is the truth when its modifications have ceased, so they say that the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti) is the truth when its modifications have ceased. (3.2.15)
That [universal] must be the denotable object of all words, and words are not separate from it;
yet, if they are not separate, there can be no relation between the two, as if they were distinct entities. (3.2.16)
Self, other, the beloved, the hateful, the speaker, the subject of speech, and the purpose—these opposites appear to a single person like the forms of a mind in a dream. (3.2.17)
In that which is unborn, likewise eternal, and devoid of priority and posteriority, the nature of birth and so forth is perceived as contradictory to reality. (3.2.18)
Thus concludes the summary of substances.

3.3 The Exposition of Relation (Saṃbandhasamuddeśa) When words are uttered, the knowledge of the speaker, the external object, and their own form are perceived; thus, the relation among them is firmly established. (3.3.1)
In some cases, there may be doubt for the cognizer regarding either the object or the cognition;
however, when their own forms are perceived, no deviation [from their nature] exists. (3.3.2)
"That this is the designator and that is the designated" is understood through the genitive case;
therefore, the relation between word and meaning is also designated as their *tattva* (essential identity). (3.3.3)
There is no name that, by its own nature, expresses the relationship;
because it is absolutely dependent [on other factors], its form cannot be designated. (3.3.4)
Because it is through assistance that it exists, that dharma is followed wherever it is found;
it is the power even of powers, and it is the quality even of qualities. (3.3.5)

But the application of those terms to the two [entities] possessing those properties—namely conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*)—is due to their being restricted as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the sake of mutual assistance. (3.3.6)
For indeed, there is a certain specific state, indicated by the production of an effect, in which a conjunction arises for someone with something. (3.3.7)

Regarding the production of things that lack a self, whatever restriction there is to specific instances, and the non-cessation [of that restriction] which is caused by that very [restriction] despite the lack of difference in their attainment; (3.3.8)
That by which one self is determined to be like another self, and because of which neither unity nor plurality is definitively ascertained as the reality; // 3.3.9 //
That power called "inherence" (samavāya), which assists other powers, transcends both difference and non-difference, and is established in a manner entirely distinct [from them]. (3.3.10)
The tradition from the predecessors is that *dharma*, which transcends all categories and possesses all characteristics, favors [the relationship] known as "connection" (*saṃbandha*). (3.3.11)
Others everywhere accept that the relation itself is treated as a distinct category; therefore, it is impossible to separate the relation from the meaning of the word. 3.3.12
Through inherence, its own substratum and its own genus are perceived; however, through inherence in the same object, qualities that reside in their own substratum [are perceived]. (3.3.13)
Substantiality, existence, and conjunction are bound to substrates other than themselves;
so too are their spatial divisions and those qualities such as duality and the like. (3.3.14)
Some are conjoined with their own substratum; some are inherent in that [substratum]; others are inherent in things that are themselves conjoined and inherent. (3.3.15)
But it is understood that the all-pervading [entity] is conjoined with those things conjoined with its own substratum;
no further relation of inherence is observed there. (3.3.16)
Since the relationship [between word and object] would be indistinguishable, there could be no restriction here;
therefore, the relationship between word and object is not conceived in this manner. (3.3.17)

Just as the conjunction of the self with something else occurs through the acquisition of the operation of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)—known as the relation between owner and owned in some cases—this same sequence applies elsewhere even where there is no difference [between the two]. (3.3.18)
But the speaker or the listener does not, by means of words, apprehend that "attainment" (prāpti) called "inherence" (samavāya), which transcends the properties of the objects denoted. (3.3.19)
When that which is expressible as "inexpressible" is determined to be expressible by virtue of its inexpressibility, then it becomes indeed expressible. (3.3.20)
Moreover, even if one thinks, "It is inexpressible," that which is intended to be expressed is not understood as such;
for the very state of the object that one wishes to convey is not determined. (3.3.21)
Even in that case where it is asserted that something is inexpressible in such a way, otherwise, or in every respect, that very state is not at all negated by those words. (3.3.22)

For when an object in the form of doubt has been established as a subordinate element (śeṣa), another doubt regarding its own nature does not arise so long as that [initial] doubt has not been dispelled. (3.3.23)
And when a determination is undertaken as a determination within the cognition of determination, then that cognition abides by its own characteristic. (3.3.24)
The statement "I speak everything falsely" is not intended to be expressed [as a literal truth]; for if that were stated falsely, the matter under discussion would not be understood. (3.3.25)
And that which functions in the form of a signifier cannot itself be the signified; for that by which something else is understood cannot itself be the object to be understood therein. (3.3.26)
It is not merely that this proposition is stated to be unestablished;
rather, in the same manner, no property whatsoever is perceived here [in it]. (3.3.27)
Since there is no further operation whatsoever for an operation, one should therefore never resort to contradiction or infinite regress in any case. (3.3.28)
Just as the capacity of the sense organs for their respective objects is beginningless, so too is the relationship between words and their meanings—their capacity—beginningless. (3.3.29)
Some maintain that an incorrect word is expressive through inference;
or, even if there is no difference in their expressiveness, there is a restriction regarding merit and demerit. (3.3.30)
