In the case of a word denoting a relation, the relation [is established] with respect to fitness; fitness is [known] through me (the self), just like the connection between mother and son and so forth. (3.3.31)
Sound is the cause of meaning, for it is produced by that [meaning]; and likewise, sound is cognized from the object which is the domain of cognition. (3.3.32)
Even things such as food are considered to exist for the sake of cognition when they are impossible [to perceive otherwise];
for once that which exists for the sake of cognition has arisen from the very fact of being for the sake of cognition, even that [food] is seen [as such]. (3.3.33)
Even in things that are impermanent, permanence exists by way of the nature of the denotable object;
or else, impermanence is its own power, and that [power] does not differ from the permanent. (3.3.34)
The refinement of the meaning by means of the word is performed for the sake of visible and invisible purposes;
how could that occur without a relationship [between the two]? (3.3.35)
Such a refinement (saṃskāra) is not necessarily observed in the objects denoted;
nor is such a relationship as intended [by the proponent] actually seen to exist. (3.3.36)
The relation [between word and meaning] is established as the state of being a causal condition;
for it is from this that it is understood that the relation exists there, in the word with respect to its object. (3.3.37)
Whether the object be eternal or non-eternal, how could a person ever be able to establish a relationship between it and words whose own relationships have not already been established? (3.3.38)
In the designation of categories, the existence of others is metaphorical;
it reveals the nature of the self of all things in all their states. (3.3.39)
Just as a substance such as crystal, through its own inherent power, enters into a relationship with various colored substrates as if it were identical in form to them; (3.3.40)
In the same way, the word also, having previously been established in pure existence (sattā), enters into relation with properties that are both non-contradictory and contradictory. (3.3.41)
And thus, when the objects to be negated are relied upon through metaphorical designation for the sake of establishing the negation, the negation proceeds. (3.3.42)
The acquisition of self-nature is called "birth," and that which exists is what is acquired.
If it already exists, how can it be born? Or if it does not exist, how can it be born? (3.3.43)

For the going of a goer proceeds only when there is an object to be gone over; if it were like the case of the goer, the purpose of birth would not exist, and if it were not like that, one is not born. (3.3.44)

However, for the sake of the application of verbal designation, one metaphorically treats the agent as the object; and then again, one treats that action—which has that [agent] as its substratum—as having the status of an object. (3.3.45)
Therefore, in that case, the suffixes *la* and others must be understood as expressing a metaphorical existence (*upacāra-sattā*);
for a primary existence (*mukhyā sattā*) does not exist there, because it is contradictory to [the fact of] birth. (3.3.46)
Sustaining itself by itself, it is designated as "it exists";
and because that [self] is included within that very action, it is not transitive. (3.3.47)
And prior to the connection with existence, how could there be primary existence?
Furthermore, that which is non-existent cannot be the agent of the verb "to exist"; however, figurative usage may occur as before. (3.3.48)

Therefore, among distinct and contradictory phenomena, there exists a non-contradictory [nature] which is resorted to by various words solely for the purpose of making that contradiction known. (3.3.49)
[The word-meaning] exists at a single time across objects that exist at different times;
it is the cause of the application of all words, and its status as such is figurative. (3.3.50)
For no object whatsoever transcends this existence;
and that [existence] has been shown in the Bhāṣya to be distinct from present existence. (3.3.51)
Whether it be a portion of a region, or a determination from another [source], or a contrary state, or non-existence—it is upon these that linguistic convention proceeds. (3.3.52)

Just as a cognition arising from objects occurs as if possessing a superimposition of a measure due to a defect in the sense faculty, so too does the cognition born of mere enumeration arise. (3.3.53)
Relying upon a cognition in which its object does not appear in its entirety, the word expresses the object through another form, while its own form remains unascertained. (3.3.54)
On the worldly path, both the fool and the wise man are alike in their susceptibility to transformation and designation, as well as in their cognition and verbal expression. (3.3.55)
The purity of gnosis consists in its being the nature of all objects and its being without support; some, moreover, speak of its supreme purity as being formless. (3.3.56)
For the conformity to external forms is indeed an affliction of knowledge; like turbidity, it arises from contact with that [external object] through a process of mutual blending. (3.3.57)
And just as cognition, due to its representation, remains fixed upon impurity, so too the object, by virtue of its dependence [on that cognition], is distanced from its own true nature. (3.3.58)
Thus, when there is a discrepancy regarding the object, the word, and the cognition, existence and non-existence follow conventional usage without distinction. (3.3.59)
Just as the non-existence of something is understood by relying on its existence, so too the existence of that thing is understood by relying on its non-existence. (3.3.60)
Non-existence does not become existence, nor does existence pass into the state of the ineffable;
for existence and non-existence are merely conceptual constructs, not different from the single Self. (3.3.61)
Because non-existence is indefinable, a cause cannot establish it;
but as for existence, which is definable, what could a cause possibly do for it? (3.3.62)
Therefore, everything is asserted to be either non-existence or existence; there is no other state whatsoever that exists as something distinct from the single reality. (3.3.63)
Therefore, those in the world who are proponents of existence do not accept non-existence, nor do the proponents of non-existence accept existence as the defining characteristic of reality. (3.3.64)
And although everything is non-dual and possesses a single characteristic by its very nature, a manifold variety of boundaries is perceived within conceptual constructions. (3.3.65)
For just as four states have been conceptually constructed regarding that which is indefinable, so too this twofold nature [of existence and non-existence] is based upon being and non-being. (3.3.66)
Whether non-contradictory or contradictory, existent or even non-existent according to reason, whether possessing succession or lacking succession, non-existence is not logically tenable. (3.3.67)

Whether it be non-contradictory or contradictory, existent or even non-existent in reality, whether possessing succession or lacking succession—by that [analysis], no entity (bhāva) is found to exist. (3.3.68)
In the absence of non-existence, the possibility of difference across the three times does not exist;
that being absent, even existence cannot be established across the three times. (3.3.69)
The abandonment of the reality of the self is not possible through another; moreover, the reality of the self is not tenable either through another or through itself. (3.3.70)
In reality, there is no contradiction; in plurality, there is no assistance whatsoever.
When both identity and difference are relinquished, conventional discourse ceases. (3.3.71)
Those who know the Upanishads (the end of the three Vedas) take refuge in the reality of that very object wherein the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing are non-conceptualized. (3.3.72)
Since words denote either a universal or a particular as possessing distinctions, they are established only upon those very differences which are unreal. (3.3.73)
For when non-existence exists, the self of existence is not abandoned;
nor does the self of existence arise when non-existence is absent. (3.3.74)
The existence of the brindled cow does not sublate the existence of the black cow; nor is it on the grounds that "the brindled cow does not exist" that the black cow is conceptualized. (3.3.75)
If non-existence were a real entity, then this investigation would apply to it; and even in the absence of that [entity], this [investigation] would have to be carried out once again. (3.3.76)
That which has passed away would be a non-entity if it were the object of conventional discourse;
in that case, a distinction residing in a real entity cannot be meaningfully expressed. (3.3.77)
In a case where there is no basis for an object, the application of a causal factor is not found;
yet, when a cause exists, the prior non-existence of that object is observed. (3.3.78)
"What was its prior state?"—this [question] relies upon a real entity (vastu).
Furthermore, this "prior state" does not exist; for neither of these two [states] exists in a non-entity (avastu). (3.3.79)
There is no basis for stating that "it exists" or "it does not exist" regarding what is above [the world]; they declare this to be a state beyond the reach of speech. (3.3.80)
But this process is truly marvelous: that the essential nature (ātmatattva) of entities—which previously did not exist, which have no parts, and which are without sequence—is revealed. (3.3.81)
All worldly linguistic usage is carried out by means of entities produced solely by conceptual construction, just as it is by primary referents. (3.3.82)
Therefore, proponents of eternalism consider this [succession] to be the power of the entity itself;
they say that succession is the entity alone, for there is no succession other than the entity. (3.3.83)
In reality, there is no distinction whatsoever between succession and simultaneity;
just as non-existence is not determined to be anything other than existence itself. (3.3.84)
Ordinary people indeed designate even one time as another time;
yet, by mere designation, a real distinction is not established. (3.3.85)
Constructing a basis through the intellect, one does not settle for the absence [of such a basis]; for even regarding non-entities, no one's imaginative construction is ever obstructed. (3.3.86)
Therefore, through the differentiation of its powers, a single eternal object, consisting of both being and non-being, appears in many forms when it is expressed by words. (3.3.87)

The worldly transaction of people proceeds by means of conceptualized categories; in the treatise, however, a worldly category is analytically distinguished for the sake of accomplishing a specific purpose. (3.3.88)
Thus concludes the Summary of Relations.
3.4 Enumeration of Substances:

Arising from the form of the composite whole and extracted from the form of consciousness, substances are analyzed in the treatise from the meaning of the sentence, just as the meanings of stems and suffixes are distinguished from the meaning of a word. 3.4.1.
Certain categories of meaning, which serve as the basis for grammatical correctness and whose nature is inferred from the treatise, will be explained here in brief according to tradition. (3.4.2)
That object where all names are applied, being intended as something to be differentiated, is called a "substance" (dravya). (3.4.3)
Thus ends the summary of the further substances.
3.5 Exposition of Qualities (guṇasamuddeśa):

Whatever is perceived as being in contact [with a substance], as being a differentiator, and as possessing an operation, its status as a quality is declared in the treatise because of its dependence on another. 3.5.1.

When a quality is taken up for the purpose of distinguishing an otherwise indescribable substance, that excellence [of the quality] which serves as the means of designation is called *prakarsa*. (3.5.2)
For every primary entity, there is no excellence without a cause of distinction; nor does such excellence ever become the denotation of a word. (3.5.3)
Not all causes of differentiation, though present in the primary substances, are expressed by specific words that denote excluded objects. (3.5.4)
If a specific distinction were operative in the perception of the object there, then excellence would be without a cause, as there would be no restrictive rule. (3.5.5)
And everything is necessarily drawn away from every side by an associated cause, whether it be inferior or superior. (3.5.6)
If it does not depend on a cause that is operative toward excellence, then the material cause of a substance would be useless with respect to that excellence. (3.5.7)
Therefore, the quality, possessing its own operation and based upon its own excellence, indeed differentiates the substance itself by establishing that excellence within it. (3.5.8)
Just as a substance that lacks form is designated by means of another form, so too is a quality that lacks excellence characterized by means of excellence. (3.5.9)
Thus concludes the exposition of the qualities.
3.6 The General Exposition of Direction:
"Direction, means of proof, action, and time"—these [categories] denote real entities that are utterly unstable within the nature of the potencies of things. (3.6.1)

The cause of exclusion (*vyatireka*) between the limit (*avadhi*) and that which is to be conveyed (*pratipādya*) is such that, by means of it, cognition proceeds directly, as if [the object were] right there, even in the absence of anything else. (3.6.2)
That power upon which the manifestation of the various distinctions of action depends, being differentiated by its own limiting conditions, is called *diś* (direction). (3.6.3)

The priority and posteriority of material objects, which are based on spatial difference, are determined from that very [spatial relation]; however, their forms as a temporal sequence are determined by time.
By means of its spatial divisions and other distinct parts, that [ether] serves as the limiting adjunct for conjunctions and disjunctions. (3.6.5)
There is no fixed spatial arrangement of directions for locations; indeed, the powers of entities are manifested through their mutual assistance. (3.6.6)

Direction, which is essentially a form of conceptual construction applied to entities, is designated as "east" because it is the cognition of being "prior"; otherwise, it would be a mere conventional name. (3.6.7)
In the world, the determination of directions based on one's own limbs is not fixed; for that which is behind a person facing west becomes the front when they turn around. (3.6.8)
The restriction of spatial arrangement is not fixed among the directions; even that which is established as "western" is designated as "eastern. (3.6.9)

Therefore, because it has already expressed the masculine gender, the application of the *puṃvadbhāva* rule is not established; for in this sense, the act of procreation is never expressed by the word [in its feminine form]. (3.6.10)

But when there is the denotation of the power of direction, the perception of "east" and so forth is necessarily restricted to a specific direction, just as the determination of "sixty" is restricted to the lifespan. (3.6.11)
Through shadow and light, a distinction of parts is conceived in mountains and such; however, in entities that do not possess those properties, a distinction of parts cannot be conceived. (3.6.12)
A division of the partless atom is posited by means of spatial direction; they call that the primary capacity for the conceptualization of parts. (3.6.13)
Entities are indeed without location, without parts, without emergence, and without support;
yet, through their form as associated with others, a differentiation of capacities is conceptualized. (3.6.14)
The nature of being partless is the same for both an atom and a jar; any "part" therein is merely a difference in capacity, as is their respective magnitude. (3.6.15)
Since difference is conceptualized from that [unity], difference is also observed therein;
therefore, the wise know that a difference whose cessation is unobserved is most illogical. (3.6.16)
Because that effect is observed everywhere, it is held to be all-pervading (vibhu);
they say this alone is its omnipresence, while for others there is the rule of possessing a body.
The conceptualization of space and time exists in the world like consciousness itself;
for who indeed could establish that nature of living beings otherwise? (3.6.18)
There would be a confusion of legal procedures if there were a reversal of the natural order;
therefore, by abandoning these states of being, one takes hold of them once again. (3.6.19)
But the distinction of that power as "east" and so forth is based on other entities;
thus, direction, being differentiated by that distinction, serves only to produce further differentiation. (3.6.20)

And when there is a connection with the requirement of a limit (*avadhi*), the rule characterized by direction (*diglakṣaṇa*) applies; for instance, in the case of "the east" (*pūrvaḥ*), the genitive case alone is observed when it refers to another property (*dharmāntara*). (3.6.21)
Furthermore, a reversal of the directions such as east and so forth is never observed when there is no confusion regarding the limits [of the directions];
and this indicative mark—that "this belongs to him" in a straightforward manner—is not subject to transposition. (3.6.22)
Or rather, a property of the internal organ manifests externally in this manner;
however, in this [ultimate] process, the distinction between internal and external does not exist. (3.6.23)

Having understood that the conceptualization of these powers as being either one or many falls into the realm of non-reality, one should not grasp at them as true from the perspective of ultimate reality. (3.6.24)
Since linguistic conventions regarding entities—which transcend conceptual construction—are based upon social agreements, worldly practice follows them in those matters. (3.6.25)
There is no unity without multiplicity, nor is there the other without unity;
in the ultimate sense, this distinction between the two does not exist at all. (3.6.26)

The distinction between powers is not as great as the distinction between the possessors of power; nor does that worldly unity which exists among the possessors exist within the powers themselves. (3.6.27)
Unity would not be established if one did not conceive of multiplicity;
and multiplicity would be lost if one did not conceive of unity. (3.6.28)
Thus concludes the summary of the directions.

3.7 Exposition of the Means (Sādhanasamuddeśa) They know that the means (*sādhana*) is the capacity for the accomplishment of actions, which reside in their own substratum and likewise [in] other substrata. (3.7.1)

Because the world, which possesses manifold properties, always exists in every way, the possessor of power [the speaker] intends to express only this or that [aspect] in a particular instance. (3.7.2)
And the practice of establishing [the existence of things] is based on the states of the intellect;
whether existing or non-existing among the forms of objects, a distinction is conceptually constructed by the intellect. (3.7.3)
When a speaker, having first conceived the unity of the Pañcālas with the Kurus through the intellect,
subsequently divides them again, then disappearance (apāya) is perceived.

And one regards Kaṃsa and others—who have had their forms imparted by words and have thus become objects of cognition—as if they were directly perceived, as being the means [of accomplishment]. (3.7.5)
And by superimposing the form of the activity of the intellect upon objects, speakers construct the conceptualization of distinct powers within those objects. (3.7.6)

When the individual object (*vyakti*) is the referent of the word, the status of being a means (*sādhana*) for the action being produced—such as [the utterance of] the word—is likewise established as being conceptually constructed (*prakalpita*) from the form of cognition (*buddhirūpa*). (3.7.7)
Independence and dependence, as well as the nature of sequence, have been shown to be based on conceptual construction even regarding entities that are devoid of activity. (3.7.8)
For those who maintain the theory of inherence (*saṃsarga*), all entities consist of both powers (*śakti*) and power-possessors (*śaktimat*);
it is within these entities, when they are not denoted by their own specific names, that their status as a means (*sādhanatva*) is determined. (3.7.9)
When the jar is the object of the act of seeing, its qualities such as magnitude (mahattva) and so forth are the means of perception;
when color is the object of the act of seeing, its qualities such as color-ness (rūpatva) and so forth are the means of perception.

In the world, the flavors and other [qualities], being endowed with their own general and particular potencies, have restricted apprehensions; those potencies are likewise [restricted] by their substrates. (3.7.11)
In some cases, the means of accomplishment is the connection between the sense organ, the object, the mind, and the agent;
whatever assists something at a particular time, that is the means of accomplishment for it at that time. (3.7.12)
But when expressed by its own words, that property is not denoted;
rather, this assistance is understood through the case-endings and so forth alone. (3.7.13)

The state of being a sign (nimittabhāva) of entities is resorted to for the sake of assistance; thus, "inclination" (nati) and "bending toward" (āvarjanā) are established as the means of accomplishment (sādhana). (3.7.14)
Whether it is distinct from them or their very self, it is conceived as a means of accomplishment by relying upon its distinction [from them]. (3.7.15)
Manifestation [of the self] occurs in the state of aspiration; however, it follows immediately upon the state of resolve.
Likewise, resolve serves as the means for the commencement of action. (3.7.16)
The very same action that exists in the former [subject] is considered the means in the latter; however, in the act of perception, they know consciousness itself to be the specific means. (3.7.17)

The status of being an agent exists in every factor of action (kāraka) simply by virtue of its accomplishment [of the result]; however, when there is a requirement for distinctions in their respective operations, the status of being an instrument (karaṇa) and so forth becomes possible. (3.7.18)
Just as the agency of the parents in the birth of a son is expressed by the distinction intended for communication: "This [son] is in her" and "She is from him. (3.7.19)
The agents of qualities and actions have their powers suppressed by the primary agent; yet even when thus suppressed, they remain endowed with their own complete functions. (3.7.20)
Known as instruments and so forth through their participation in various actions, they subsequently attain autonomy and reach the state of being agents with respect to the primary action. (3.7.21)
Just as the status of being a warrior resides in those warriors appointed by a king, it is upon their conduct that the king incurs victory or defeat. (3.7.22)
Likewise, when all [factors] are directed by an agent and perform a single purpose, the status of being an agent does not contradict their subsequent status as instruments and so forth. (3.7.23)
But when the operation does not depend [on another], it is accepted as a cause (*hetu*);
whereas those who know define that which depends on the state of being a limit (*avadhi*) as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). (3.7.24)
The cause (*hetu*) has as its object substance (*dravya*) and so forth; the agent (*kāraka*) is that whose action is restricted.
An agent who depends on another agent is intended to be the cause with respect to an action. (3.7.25)
An instrument is observed to exist for the sake of an action; likewise, a substitute for it is seen.
However, since an action has the cause as its purpose, that [cause] is not substituted. (3.7.26)

The reason (hetu) establishes the object (artha) through both the reverse and the direct order; its being for that purpose (tādarthya) follows the direct order, while its nature as a reason follows the reverse order. (3.7.27)
The innate power exists everywhere, persisting as long as the substance itself;
however, at the time of action, it is beneficial through its manifestation based on its substrate. (3.7.28)
A wall has the power to obstruct, while swords and the like have the power to cleave; yet that property, though always present, is only discerned at the time of its activity. (3.7.29)
Just as the nooses of Varuṇa attached to the bodies of the Daityas are manifested,
so too are the powers of substances revealed when they seek to conquer.
When the sword, by means of its own sharpness, weight, hardness, and shape, is applied toward that which is to be cut, it is then perceived as possessing power. (3.7.31)
Some maintain that the means of accomplishment (sādhana) arises prior to the action from another cause; some hold it to be innate; and others maintain that it exists before the action. (3.7.32)
Activity itself, at first independent of anything else, draws forth the powers within a single substratum like a flowing stream. (3.7.33)
Some say that this entity characterized in such a way is either an unprecedented power of time, or an action, or time itself; and why should they not? (3.7.34)
For others, six powers are eternal and endowed with both difference and non-difference;
they are inherent in objects for the sake of the accomplishment of action, just like a genus (jāti). (3.7.35)
And these [powers], through distinctions such as substance, form, and so forth, appear as if they were infinite; however, their reality does not transcend six powers. (3.7.36)
Due to the difference in signs (nimitta), the single power (śakti) is perceived as divided; they say that agency itself is sixfold, being the basis for its manifestation. (3.7.37)
Whether it be identity or difference, that [object] is said to be distinct;
the world has verbal testimony as its authority, and it is followed by the treatise. (3.7.38)
But in the ultimate sense, there is no oneness characterized as distinct from difference;
rather, reality itself manifests through the forms of both difference and oneness. (3.7.39)
That which is undoubtedly distinct does not differ from unity;
that which is undoubtedly one does not differ from distinctness. (3.7.40)
Heaven, earth, wind, the sun, the oceans, the rivers, and the directions are the external manifestations of the reality of the internal organ. (3.7.41)
That very same single entity persists in the form of temporal divisions;
for that being, which has neither beginning nor end, is perceived in the form of a sequence. (3.7.42)

For even in the absence of non-difference, a difference is observed; and even in the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there is the concomitance of the referents such as "tree. Therefore, the meaning of the case-ending is held to be distinct [from the nominal stem]. (3.7.43)
The general factor of action (kāraka) has seven primary sources of differentiation;
six are distinguished by the categories beginning with "object" (karman), while the seventh is the remaining category, the locative (saptamī).
The domain of the object (*karmādhikāra*) is considered to be threefold: that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is reached (*prāpya*).
Among these, the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) is the primary *karman*, while the other four types are conceptualized as distinct. (3.7.45)

That which is obtained through indifference, that which is not desired by the agent, that which is not designated by other technical names, and that which has another as its antecedent—[these are the four kinds of *udāsīna*]. (3.7.46)
Whether it exists or does not exist, that whose changing nature (prakṛti) is not relied upon is declared to be "that which is to be produced" (nirvartya). (3.7.47)
However, when the material cause (*prakṛti*) is intended to be expressed, some maintain that it is the "object of transformation" (*vikārya*);
furthermore, in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), the object (*karman*) is shown to be both "that which is to be produced" (*nirvartya*) and "that which is to be transformed" (*vikārya*). (3.7.48)

That which is non-existent and comes into being, or that which already exists and is manifested through birth—such an object is established as twofold: the *nirvartya* (that which is produced) and the *vikārya* (that which is modified). (3.7.49)
Some [destruction] arises from the cutting off of its original nature, like the ashes of wood and the like;
some arises through the production of another quality, like the transformation of gold and the like. (3.7.50)
When the accomplishment of specific qualities through action is not perceived either by direct observation or by inference, that is said to be "attainable" (prāpya). (3.7.51)
A special attainment exists everywhere through seeing and other means;
for some, there is the accomplishment of its manifestation, as seen in the case of those with poisonous gazes and the like. (3.7.52)
Appearance, manifestation, and endurance—these are the specific stages of an action as it is being accomplished, established for the purpose of achieving the result. (3.7.53)

Having first experienced independence in the case of things to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth, it subsequently becomes the object (*karman*) in relation to the operations of other agents. (3.7.54)

Even when the activity of that [subordinate] has ceased, it remains established in its own activity; in certain cases, it receives injunctions based on scripture that are prescribed for the sake of the primary action. (3.7.55)
When the instigation has ceased, the object remains within its own constituent action; as its status as an object ceases, it persists in its status as an agent. (3.7.56)
The wise understand those other elements to be like the words *paci*, *sidhyati*, and so on;
even though there is a difference [in their specific functions], they are conceived as one because their essential form is the same. (3.7.57)
Verbs such as *pac* (to cook) and others, possessing identical forms, function by their very nature with respect to both a single part and the aggregate of actions. (3.7.58)

The causative sense of "subduing" (*nyagbhāvanā*) and "the state of being subdued" (*nyagbhavana*) is understood when the root *ruh* is in its simple form; it is also recognized when the root is in its *ṇic*-causative form. (3.7.59)
They call that the fifth state when [the root] ends in the causative suffix (ṇic) and functions as a reflexive agent (karmakartṛ).
When the causative suffix (ṇic) is said to express its original meaning after the sense of instigation has ceased, [that is this state]. (3.7.60)
The root *sidh* expresses the meaning of *pac* (to cook) without the suffix *ṇic*;
that [root] ending in *ṇic* is established in the primary sense of *pac*. (3.7.61)

The operation belonging to certain agents such as Devadatta, which [involves] an object when [the verb is] transitive, is intended to be expressed without [mentioning] Devadatta and others when it concerns objects such as mats. (3.7.62)

When the instigation has ceased, the object becomes the instigator of its own agent; when it is connected with another instigation, it is expressed by the *ṇic* affix in the causative form (*ṇyanta*). (3.7.63)

In cases such as "similar" (*sadṛśa*), where the status of object and agent is attained, there the two actions—namely, the reaching (*āpatti*) and the causing to reach (*āpādane*)—have the [object] as their respective domains. (3.7.64)

If one were to bring in a word from somewhere else and thus construct [the meaning] in this way, then those words denoting seeing and so forth would have the status of being bhāvas residing in the object (karmasthabhāvaka). (3.7.65)
Wherever there is a perception of distinction, action is established therein; however, for others, the establishment of action is manifested by words alone. (3.7.66)

When time (kāla), state (bhāva), distance (adhvan), and place (deśa) are connected with all verbs that have become transitive through the inclusion of another action within them, they acquire the status of an object (karma). (Pāṇini 2.3.5)

Having attained, as it were, the status of a locus (*ādhāra*) with respect to substances and actions, time and the other factors subsequently enter into a different category, namely, the status of the object (*karman*). (3.7.68)

Therefore, the verbal root (dhātu), when conjoined with those [karmakartṛ] actions which are not [inherently] objects, becomes intransitive; it is thus fit to serve as the cause for the *la* suffix to express both the object and the state of being (*bhāva*). (3.7.69)

And every unspoken object of action is understood to belong to a different category [from the primary object], because it differs in its relation to the goal of the verbal root's meaning; indeed, that is not considered the "most desired" (īpsitatama). (3.7.70)

That which prompts an action is called the primary object (*pradhānakarman*); however, another [object] connected with the action for the sake of accomplishing that [primary one] is traditionally known as the "unspoken" (*akathita*) object. (3.7.71)

In verbs such as *nī* ("to lead"), the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is based on the fact that it is not specifically mentioned (*akathāśraya*), just as it is in the case of verbs like *duh* ("to milk").
However, when the verb *ākhyā* ("to tell") is used with the sense of "informing" (*anupayoga*), the remaining [object] is intended by the restrictive rule [Pāṇini 1.4.51].

For roots such as *duh* (to milk) and others which have the meaning of the causative (*ṇic*) inherent within them, the status of being an object is established by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 1.4.49] just as it is for those ending in *ṇic*; likewise, the restriction regarding those ending in *ṇic* applies here.
Just as there is no basis for excellence within the category of the instrument itself, so too there would be no superiority within the category of the object itself. (3.7.74)

But since it is accepted that action is desired for the sake of attainment, and since a distinction is thereby resorted to, there is consequently an absolute difference from the previous type of action. (3.7.75)

And just as in the case of a causative verb (*ṇijanta*), the agent, being active, is employed [as the subject], so too in roots such as *duh* (to milk), the agent is employed even though he is inactive. (3.7.76)

But as for the statement regarding the distinction—that which occurs when the root ends in *ṇi*, and that which occurs in the case of the roots *nī* and *duh*—because they are different words, there is no contact whatsoever between them and the verbal root. (3.7.77)
Just as a single *apādāna* is shown with its divisions in the treatise, so too a single *karman* is explained through its various classifications. (3.7.78)

Whether it is something to be produced (*nirvartya*), modified (*vikārya*), or attained (*prāpya*), that which is the locus of the means of accomplishment is designated as having an established form (*siddharūpa*), because it is the actions themselves that are to be accomplished (*sādhya*). (3.7.79)
Just as a desire arises in an agent toward harmful things due to greed, so too does that [desire] proceed toward poisons and the like due to fear and other such causes. (3.7.80)
Where there is a separate capacity for the substance and the two actions—primary and secondary—the quality depends upon that which is primary. (3.7.81)

When the capacity whose primary object is the principal element is expressed by a suffix, then that [capacity], although not explicitly stated when it pertains to a subordinate element, is nevertheless manifested. (3.7.82)

When an action not previously mentioned is expressed by a suffix ending in *ktvā* denoting a state (*bhāva*), that action appears as having the same properties [as the main verb], even when it is stated to have a different capacity (*śakti*) than the act of eating. (3.7.83)
And because of the contact between the root *iṣ* (to desire) and the root *gam* (to go), the suffix *lo* which is prescribed [after *gam*] when it means "village" is employed;
therein, the object of the action of going is experienced by the desirer alone. (3.7.84)
In the expression "it is eaten after being cooked," for some [grammarians], the verb *pacati* ("he cooks") does not require an object; that object is understood through inference. (3.7.85)

Likewise, the action that is expressed by a verbal suffix ending in *tiṅ* when it denotes the object of an adherence (*abhiniveśa*)—even though it is also an *adhikaraṇa* (locus) when ending in *ktvā*—they do not desire the locative case (*saptamī*) there. (3.7.86)

Furthermore, that action which has already produced its basis (the body) but has not yet been accumulated through acquisition, is intended [as the object of the rule] when it is differentiated by the occurrence of objects such as food and so forth. (3.7.87)

An action is considered intransitive (akarmika) due to the root's application in a different sense, its inclusion within the meaning of the verbal root itself, established usage, or the lack of intention to express the object. (3.4.88)
These four types of division which have been shown in general are further divided in many ways according to the distinctions of causes and so forth. (3.7.89)
Thus concludes the section on karma.
The section on the instrument (*karaṇa*):
when, in the accomplishment of an action, that whose operation immediately precedes it is intended to be expressed [as such], then its status as the instrument is traditionally taught. (3.7.90)
In reality, that [agenthood] is indefinable, for no entity exists as fixed; since we observe the intended meaning in such expressions as "the pot cooks. (3.7.91)
But with respect to the instruments, they repeatedly initiate refinement and specific applications for the sake of accomplishing the primary purpose. (3.7.92)

Furthermore, there is no excellence of the instruments within their own respective spheres; rather, the characteristic of excellence in that case is the attainment of superiority through dependence on something else. (3.7.93)
Even when [the agent] possesses independence, the users [of the instrument] assist only from afar;
for the operation of all [agents] is mediated by the instrument. (3.7.94)

This excellence [of the instrument] exists in the accomplishment of the action, while the agent indeed remains subordinate; for when the action is accomplished, the general property of being an "accomplisher" (sādhakatva) is intensified. (3.7.95)
When the sword and so forth are the agents, they know sharpness and the like to be the instruments;
when sharpness and the like are independent, the self is established in two ways. (3.7.96)
Even though there is a difference in the individual selves, that single object remains as it is;
because the agency resides in that [object], even given the difference [between selves], agency [in the self] is therefore sublated. (3.7.97)
Just as instrumentality is understood through proximity, so too is it understood through the accomplishment of the action even in the absence of proximity. (3.7.98)

They explain that the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) belongs to "a little" (stoka) and so forth, either because of the accomplishment of that [action] by means of a small amount, or because of its non-accomplishment. (3.7.99)
In the same way, [the cognition] is distinguished by the difference and non-difference of the properties (dharmas) possessing them;
it is differentiated by the specific delimitation of the limit of the action, just as in the case of [the cognition of] an action. (3.7.100)
Thus ends the section on the instruments of action.

The section on the agent [is established] prior to [the acquisition of power from] another, because of the subordination [of others], because those who have begun their activity proceed under its control, and because it causes them to desist. (3.7.101)

Because no substitute is observed [for the agent], and because [the result] is seen even in the absence [of the agent], the independence of the agent is asserted, even though [the action] is beneficial from afar. (3.7.102)
Restriction applies to the word through the properties [of its denotation] that have arisen, but not to the actual object;
when there is a desire to express a property of the agent, the agent is understood from the word. (3.7.103)
When a distinction is conceptually constructed for a single entity through its various cognitive states, the status of agent, instrument, and object arises. (3.7.104)
The non-existence prior to origination is based on a state of cognition;
it is indistinguishable from other existing things, yet it becomes the agent of birth. (3.7.105)
When the cause does not remain distinct from the state of the effect, it then acquires the designation "effect" and arises as an effect. (3.7.106)
Just as a serpent takes on a coiled form or as scattered parts become a whole, so too do some declare that the nature of existence for the virtuous is birth. (3.7.107)
Whatever effect proceeds from its causes with distinct origins, its own genus also remains established in the form of individual manifestations. (3.7.108)
The placement of the foot belongs only to entities, whether it be that of wisdom or of speech;
even the statement "it does not exist" does not apply to what is non-existent, nor is existence differentiated from that [non-existence]. (3.7.109)
The intellect and words function with respect to entities as they truly are;
there exists no conventional usage for them by means of any other reality. (3.7.110)
Just as there is the differentiation of space and the movement of a shadow, so too have birth and destruction been imagined by some, even though there is no actual division [in reality]. (3.7.111)
Just as the non-existence of space is unreal when defined by a material form, so too the non-existence of a material form is unreal when dependent upon space. (3.7.112)
Just as the essence of action is designated by means of its objects and activities, this sequence of cause and effect arises from the perception of their non-difference. (3.7.113)

Regarding the doubt as to whether the agent of birth is the modification (*vikāra*) or the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the views of various proponents differ according to their observations of indicative marks. (3.7.114)

When the fourth case ending is used in the sense of "becoming" (*saṃpadyamāna*), it expresses a modification (*vikāra*); for example, the statement regarding a gold ball as the material cause (*prakṛti*) with reference to the earring (*kuṇḍala*). (3.7.115)
In the sentence, the agent of the verb *sampad* is said to be a "group" (*saṅgha*) when it ends in the suffix *cv-*;
in the derivative form, as in *saṅghībhavanti*, the Brāhmaṇas possess independence. (3.7.116)

That which attains the state of "you" (the personal pronoun *tvam*) is not you; therefore, the activity of the person (*puruṣa*) does not reside in that which is the substratum of "you. That [state] is designated as belonging to primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (3.7.117)
Not abandoning its prior state while touching upon a subsequent dharma, the essence of an entity, as if swooning, is designated as "being born. (3.7.118)
In some cases, a certain property is perceived as being more actively engaged in an operation; moreover, the powers of entities, though distinct, may become conjoined. (3.7.119)
In the case of error, it would be understood as the person's engagement with a contrary object;
for here, the means of cognition is perceived as being accompanied by an operation. (3.7.120)
"The thought might arise there that 'you have become someone else';
just as it would be when a king has fallen into the state of a servant, so too would be the case with the transition [of the soul]. (3.7.121)
Based on the expectation that the action will be accomplished, one assumes the role of agent;
thus, in an action to be achieved by oneself, one is the instigator of the means of accomplishment. (3.7.122)
Relying solely on its own sovereignty, it remains subordinate during mere application;
thus, it becomes indistinguishable from other independent [factors] that are free from doubt. (3.7.123)
All [actions] proceed from signs for the sake of one's own welfare;
even the compliance with another's intention is for the sake of accomplishing one's own interest. (3.7.124)
Thus ends the section on the agent.

One who performs the acts of commanding or entreating, or who carries out actions conducive to those ends, attains the designation of "hetu" (cause) as prescribed by the grammatical treatise, even though he is himself the agent (*kartṛ*). (Pāṇini 1.4.55)
When there is an injunction regarding the mere substance (dravyamātra) of such words as *pṛcch* (to ask), the imperative (*loṭ*) is prescribed;
however, when that which possesses an action (*sakriya*) is employed, that is the domain of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). (3.7.126)

Having attained the status of an object (*karman*) through the act of commanding due to its independence regarding the action of a quality, it is expressed by its own grammatical property because of the restriction on the technical designation of "object. (Pāṇini 1.4.54)
An action is the instigator of another action; it is the cause of the agent and the prompter of the doer.
Furthermore, an action arises for the sake of the object through production, refinement, and attainment. (3.7.128)
Thus concludes the section on the reason (*hetu*).
The section on the recipient (saṃpradāna): That which is desired by the object of the action is a constituent part of the agent’s relinquishment because it is not rejected;
furthermore, it attains the status of a recipient through instigation or consent. (3.4.51)

Whether it functions as a cause (*hetu*), is designated as an object (*karman*), or remains as a residual factor (*śeṣa*), that which is a *kāraka* is termed "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) by the grammatical treatise in connection with verbs meaning "to please" (*rucy-artha*) and others. (Pāṇini 1.4.33–35)

And when a distinction is intended, because each subsequent subordinate element (aṅga) functions as the object (karman) with respect to each preceding action, the term "action" (kriyā) was not included [in the rule]. (3.7.131)

But when unity is intended to be expressed regarding a collection of actions, then the object, by virtue of its connection with those actions, is figuratively designated by its own name [as "action"]. (3.7.132)

The intention to express either difference or non-difference is established by its own inherent nature; therefore, no deviation is observed regarding the status of the object of a verb meaning "to go. (3.7.133)

If both [the terms *saṃjñā* and *saṃjñin*] were to exist everywhere solely by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then the rejection of the undertaking of the grammatical connection (*yoga*) would be equivalent [to its acceptance]. (3.7.134)
In that [state], action which is established as renunciation regarding what is to be abandoned and as the perception of connection regarding what is to be attained possesses a twofold form. (3.7.135)
Thus ends the section on the recipient of a gift.

The section on the ablative case (apādāna) states: "The ablative is said to be threefold: that whose object is explicitly mentioned, that whose object is implied, and that which requires an action [to be supplied]. (3.7.136)

Just as the act of going (*gati*) itself becomes "wandering" (*bhrami*) when differentiated by a change in conjunction, so too does the departure (*apāya*)—though it has a fixed limit (*dhruva*)—inhere in that which is not fixed (*adhruva*). (3.7.137)

It is understood from the Sūtra that the intrinsic nature of a substance is not permanence; rather, what is intended to be expressed is permanence as it relates to the object of its destruction. (3.7.138)
In the case of Devadatta’s refuge, there is permanence; but in the case of the horse’s fall, that which is entered by misfortune is declared to be impermanent. (3.7.139)
Although both rams are unstable even if [the action] arises from the effort of both,
the two actions are nevertheless intended to be distinguished therein when the division [of the action] is analyzed.
With respect to their respective actions, each of the two rams possesses a distinct status as a limit; and with respect to their own actions, each possesses a distinct status as an agent. (3.7.141)

If, however, a single action is intended to be expressed as being accomplished by two [agents] without distinction, then both rams are agents in the act of moving away, provided that another limit (avadhi) exists. (3.7.142)
"Without a limit (avadhi), it is not understood that there is a departure;
'the leaf of a tree falls'—thus it is illustrated in the Bhāṣya. (3.7.143)
Difference and non-difference, separateness and stability—these contradictory properties are not intended to be predicated simultaneously of all attributes in a cloud. (3.7.144)

In the expression "he pierces with a bow," since there is no intention to express separation (apāya), the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) does not exist; therefore, both [the agent and the instrument] are expressed together. (3.7.145)
Or rather, being indeed one, power remains in two forms; it is the cause for two designations therein, and the latter sublates the former. (3.7.146)

The rule concerning the ablative case used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*), as well as the rules governing words such as *bhī* ("fear") and *trā* ("protection"), involve an implied departure (*apāya*) that has been explicitly mentioned; this is intended for the comprehension of the unlearned. (3.7.147)
Thus ends the section on the ablative case (apādāna).

The section on the locus (adhikaraṇa): In this treatise, that which assists in the accomplishment of an action by supporting it indirectly—being separated from the agent and the object—is traditionally known as the locus (adhikaraṇa). (3.7.148)
In the case of sesame seeds, space, mats, and so forth, there is no difference in their contact;
however, the benefits conferred by things that are conjoined or inherent do indeed differ. (3.7.149)
The non-destruction of gravity, independence when there is an obstruction, delimitation by a specific direction, and so forth—these are the causes of differentiation. (3.7.150)
For some, space itself is considered the primary supporting power (ādhāra-śakti) of all things that possess conjunction, due to the conceptualization of spatial distinctions. (3.7.151)
Since there is no existence of entities such that "this is here," designation [of location] is not possible; they declare that to have space as its cause. (3.7.152)
From time actions are differentiated; from space all material forms arise.
This is the extent of this difference, which is nonetheless based upon non-difference. (3.7.153)
Although the term *upavāsa* (fasting) depends upon a specific location, it nevertheless refers primarily to time due to the nature of the word's application. (3.7.154)
Even when the *vasati* (staying) is not explicitly employed [as a verbal action], the location is therefore the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
Furthermore, the ritual act consisting of the three nights and so forth is traditionally recorded as being "unemployed" (*aprayukta*) in relation to the fast (*upavāsa*). (3.7.155)
Thus ends the section on the locus.
The remaining section concerns *saṃbandha* (relation), which is distinct from the *kārakas* and is preceded by action and *kārakas*.
It is designated whether the action is explicitly stated (*śrutā*) or unstated (*aśrutā*). (3.7.156)
Although it is situated in two places, because its purpose is for the sake of another, it is distinguished among the subordinate elements (*guṇa*);
being expressed therein, it also serves the primary element (*pradhāna*). (3.7.157)
The restriction of the specific occasion for the application of a term is not grasped from the word itself;
rather, that distinction is delimited by the *karmapravacanīya* particles. (Pāṇini 1.4.90)
Furthermore, when the action is heard [directly] and is designated by its instruments (sādhana), the genitive case is prescribed for every word to prevent the formation of a compound. (3.7.159)
In the case of a word ending in a kṛt-affix (niṣṭhā), the genitive case governed by the object of the action (karma-viṣayā) is also prohibited;
a compound with a genitive case used in the sense of "remainder" (śeṣa-lakṣaṇā) is not desired there. (Pāṇini 2.2.160)
When that which is designated by one [term] undergoes exclusion (vyatireka) in another [context], it acquires two properties in that different domain. (3.7.161)
Having attained primacy through its own quality, it enters into a state of subservience toward the principal;
therefore, in the case of *saha-yoga* (conjunction with "together"), its status as the principal is not lost in its own connection. (3.7.162)
Thus ends the section on the remaining topics.

The wise know that *saṃbodhana* (the vocative) is merely the manifestation of the perfected [referent] facing [the speaker]; for it is the essence of the object, having attained the state of being present, that is employed in actions. (3.7.163)
The tradition of the predecessors is that the vocative is not the meaning of the sentence;
rather, the case-meanings are extracted from the sentence-meaning by means of their respective designations. (3.7.164)
Let it be understood from the rule concerning the *avyayībhāva* compound that it applies to the meaning of a case-ending;
that meaning of a case-ending which is distinct from the substance (*dravya*) is expressed by the indeclinable (*avyaya*). (3.7.165)
But whatever substance exists in a certain way, it remains exactly so in its ultimate nature;
even when engaged in activity, its essential nature as a substance is not lost. (3.7.166)
Therefore, that substance which is an instrument could not again become an object;
otherwise, there would be a transformation of its very nature as a substance. (3.7.167)
Thus concludes the section on the means of accomplishment.
